question: Sigil of storm battlefield which says recycle a rune when you conquer. When you do this do you still gain the power from recycling it? Floating?
answer:
No — recycling the rune for Sigil of the Storm does not add Power to your pool; the Recycle action itself produces nothing.

Power only comes from activating a rune's own ability "Recycle this: [Reaction] — Add [C]" (Rule 164.2.b) — and that consumes the rune, so you can't get Power from the same rune Sigil recycles. What you can do: tap the rune for Energy first (FAQ 2810), then recycle that same rune for Sigil's trigger — the floated Energy stays in your pool for the turn. If you instead recycle a rune via its ability to bank Power, Sigil still needs a different rune to recycle; if you have none left, its trigger simply does nothing (FAQ 6863).

question: if my unit has 1 dmg on it. and the other player plays elder dragon. do they all die. or does he need to do more damage after its played?
answer:
It depends on whose damage that 1 point is.

If that 1 damage was marked by the Elder Dragon player (their spell, their combat damage, etc.), the unit dies the moment Elder Dragon enters play — no additional damage needed. Elder Dragon's passive changes the lethal threshold so that any amount of their damage is enough (Rule 142.4.c; FAQ #10686), and a cleanup check happens immediately as it enters.

If the 1 damage was dealt by you (your own spells/combat), Elder Dragon's passive doesn't touch it — it only applies to damage marked by Elder Dragon's controller. However, Elder Dragon's "When you play me" trigger deals 1 to up to one enemy unit at each location, and that 1 point is their damage, so any unit it hits will die (unless the damage is prevented, e.g., Counter Strike). So in practice: pre-existing damage from them = instant death; otherwise they still die from the ping as long as it connects.

question: Can I play vi peacekeeper in reaction to a temporal breach which targeted brynhir?
answer:
It depends on whether Brynhir's "When you play me" trigger has already resolved — and whose side you're on.

If you're an opponent of Brynhir's controller and her trigger already resolved this turn: No. "Opponents can't play cards this turn" is a blanket prohibition — it doesn't just restrict timing, it forbids playing any card at all. Vi's Ambush gives her [Reaction] timing permission, but that can't override a "can't play cards" effect (FAQ 7114: even Hidden cards are blocked).

If Brynhir's trigger is still on the chain (unresolved), or if you're Brynhir's controller (her ability only hits opponents): Yes. Temporal Breach on the chain creates a Closed State, and Vi's Ambush lets you play her as a Reaction to a battlefield you control where you have units (Rule 813.3.a). Note this doesn't stop Temporal Breach — it resolves, banishing and replaying Brynhir, which re-triggers her "When you play me," so the lockout still lands afterward.

question: Can I still trigger conquer and hold effects even when you can't score yet on forbidden waste?
answer:
Assuming you mean Forgotten Monument ("Players can't score here until their third turn") — No. While that restriction is active you cannot Conquer or Hold there, so no conquer/hold effects trigger (FAQ #4900, CR 471–473).

The key distinction: "can't score" blocks the entire scoring action (Conquering and Holding are both forms of scoring), not just the point gain. Cards like Tianna Crownguard that say "can't score points" still let the score process happen and trigger effects — but Forgotten Monument is the stricter kind, so no triggers.

One note: Forbidding Waste is a different card — it only applies a −2 Might penalty to a unit defending alone, and has no scoring restriction at all, so conquer/hold effects there trigger normally.

question: If I hold a battlefield with one unit and move it back to base, if I move another unit into that same battlefield that is now open does a showdown begin?
answer:
Yes. Moving your last unit off leaves the battlefield uncontrolled, so moving a fresh unit into it applies Contested and opens a non-combat showdown during the next cleanup (CR 344.2, 447).

Important nuance: the showdown only re-establishes your control — you do not score again at that battlefield, since you already scored it via Hold earlier this turn (CR 449; FAQ #7971). Also, unless your opponent has a unit there when it opens, it's a non-combat showdown, so no Combat Cleanup/healing occurs.

Yes — the whole line works, and Stellacorn Herder draws a card on each leg.

Moving your only unit out makes you lose control of that battlefield (CR 323.5), but a Standard Move from base to a battlefield doesn't require control of the destination (Rule 144.4). So Stellacorn Herder can still move there — that applies Contested and stages a Non-Combat Showdown, and its "When I move" trigger draws 1.

Once the showdown begins, you're the player who applied Contested, so you have Focus (Rule 345), and Rogue Assassin's Action ability is legally timed during a showdown on your turn (Rule 347.1). Activating it moves Herder back to base — that's a Move, not a Recall, so it draws a second card.

Caveats: the battlefield ends up empty and uncontrolled (no Conquer, since no unit remains when the showdown closes — and you'd already scored it via Hold this turn anyway), and you still can't play units there from hand after losing control; only moves into it are allowed.

question: If I have a shadow clone that attack 2 times in a turn will it have assault 8 or assault 4 ?
answer:
Assault 8 — if both triggers resolve.

Shadow Clone's token ability is a triggered "when I attack" that grants it Assault 4 this turn. Since that bonus lasts this turn, and Assault values from multiple sources sum (Rule 807.2), two successful triggers (banish a unit from your trash both times) give the clone Assault 4 + Assault 4 = Assault 8 while it's an attacker on the second attack. It would only be Assault 4 during the first combat.

This differs from printed Assault on cards like Lucian, which is a passive ability that simply toggles on/off each combat and doesn't accumulate. If you can't pay the banish cost on the second attack, you'd keep only the first Assault 4.

question: can you empower the same unit you disempower with profiteer
answer:
Yes — you can empower the same unit you disempower with Profiteer.

Profiteer's disempower is the cost, paid before the empower effect resolves. Disempowering removes the Empowered status (CR 443.1), so by the time you choose the empower target, that unit is no longer empowered and is a perfectly valid target. The only restriction on empowering is that you can't empower something already Empowered (CR 442.1.b–c) — disempowering first clears that.

Note the empower half of Profiteer doesn't even say "you control," so it isn't restricted to the unit you disempowered — the same unit just happens to qualify.

question: can i move a unit from one battlefield to the other with shuriken flip without ganking
answer:
Yes. Shuriken Flip's "move a friendly unit" is spell-move, not a Standard Move, so the Ganking restriction doesn't apply.

Ganking (Rule 810) only adds the battlefield→battlefield option to the Standard Move action (Rule 144.4.c). When a spell or effect moves a unit, it has none of the Standard Move limitations — no exhaust cost, no Ganking requirement, no Base↔Battlefield restriction (CR 451–451.2; FAQ #3806, #5378). So you can flip a friendly unit from one battlefield to another freely, as long as the destination isn't an invalid one (e.g., a battlefield with 2 other players' units, CR 451.2).

One caveat: "move a friendly unit" is a required target, so if you have no friendly unit in play at all, the spell is unplayable (FAQ #11682). The "Deal 2" half is optional ("up to one"), but the move is not.

question: if i control a battlefield with a hidden zhonyas and a unit. if the unit gets hit by singularity and dies can i recall zhonya's to base
answer:
No — not normally. Leave Zhonya's hidden and it's trashed when the unit dies and you lose the battlefield (CR 323.6.a). Reveal it in response to Singularity and its replacement effect is mandatory — it kills itself to save the unit (heal, exhaust, recall it to base), so Zhonya's goes to the trash, not your base.

The one exception: if the unit has Deathknell (or another death trigger that forms a chain), you get a window after it's already dead. The trigger goes on the chain during cleanup; reveal the hidden Zhonya's then. It won't save the dead unit, and as face-up unattached gear it's recalled to your base in that same cleanup (CR 459). Caveat: the Zhonya's must have been hidden on a previous turn — hidden cards have no Reaction on the turn they were hidden (Rule 811.1.b).

question: If my opponent plays Promising Future and chooses Dazzling Aurora and I choose Acceptable Losses, does Acceptable Losses kill the Dazzling Aurora?
answer:
Yes, this is due to the sequence of Promising Future.

When your opponent plays Promising Future, they decide first which card to banish (in this case Dazzling Aurora). Then you decide which to banish (Acceptable Losses).

To complete the Promising Future resolution, you put your chosen card on the chain first and as a pending item. Then the opponent does the same.

With Promising Future fully resolved we can start finalizing the pending items on the chain. This is done up the chain, first pending item gets finalized first.

So this is your Acceptable Losses. And as a spell, it lingers on the chain.

Important: Acceptable Losses does not target. It says "Each player kills one of their gear."

Second, we finalize Dazzling Aurora. And as a gear it enters play immediately.

Now with all items on the chain finalized, we can start resolving down the chain (LIFO).

Only 1 item remains on the chain though, Acceptable Losses. This resolves and its effect goes through.

If your opponent has no other gear besides Dazzling Aurora, they will be forced to kill it.

question: !ask can shady spectacles copy a unit with shady spectacles on it
answer:
Yes — you can choose a unit that has Shady Spectacles (or any gear) attached as the copy target, and the copy works normally. "Another friendly unit" has no restriction against equipped units.

The attached Shady Spectacles is not copied: gear is a separate game object, not one of the unit's printed or copied traits (FAQ #11034; Rule 479.1.b.1). Your new copy gets the source unit's copyable traits (such as Name, Type, Tags, Cost, Domain, and Rules Text) only — not its gear.

One useful nuance: if the source unit is itself already under a copy effect, you copy the traits it's currently a copy of, not the gear-carrying unit "as-is." Copying a copy gives your unit the copied traits of the source unit, which are those of the originally copied object (Rule 479.1.b). The source unit's own Shady Spectacles stays attached to it, untouched.

question: Does Disposal Order prevent me from playing Rhasa after Last Rites after already paying its cost?
answer:
No — once you've played Rhasa from trash and paid its cost, Disposal Order can't stop it.

Playing a card moves it from its zone onto the Chain in step 1 (Rule 354), so Rhasa is already on the Chain — not in your trash — before its cost is determined and paid. Disposal Order only recycles cards in opponents' trashes, so Rhasa isn't a legal choice, and recycling other cards from your trash can't retroactively raise its already-paid cost (Rule 356).

The one window that works: play Disposal Order in response to the Last Rites trigger while it's still on the chain, before it resolves. If you recycle Rhasa out of your trash then, it won't be there when Last Rites resolves and can't be played.

No. Once you've already paid Rhasa's cost, Disposal Order can't stop it — Rhasa left your trash the moment the play began (Rule 354, step 1: move to the Chain) and a finalized unit resolves immediately (Rule 337.2), so it's no longer a card "in your trash" for Disposal Order to recycle.

The window to stop it is before the Last Rites trigger resolves. Your opponent can play Disposal Order as a Reaction while the trigger is still on the Chain; if Rhasa is chosen, it gets recycled to the bottom of your deck and the trigger then finds no Rhasa in the trash to play (same logic as FAQ #11060 on Fizz). One more side note: if Disposal Order recycles 3 other cards before the trigger resolves, Rhasa's discount shrinks and it'll cost you more when you do play it — but if you've already paid, none of that applies.

question: Is playing a unit from your hand to base considered a move?
answer:
No — playing a unit from your hand to your base is not a Move.

A Move is defined as a permanent changing position between two Locations on the Board (CR 421.1, 448.1). Your hand isn't on the Board, so going hand → base is a zone change, which "does not in itself constitute a Move" (CR 448.2). That means playing a unit from hand won't trigger "when I move" effects, apply Contested, or count as a Standard Move — even though the unit ends up on the board (FAQ #5660).

question: The text in the card saying “when you play me” when can you consider a card being played?
answer:
A card is considered "played" once the act of playing it has been completed by the card resolving — not when you announce it or put it on the Chain (CR 420.4.a).

So for a unit: you put it on the Chain, it resolves and enters the battlefield, and only then does "When you play me" go on the Chain as a triggered ability. If the card is countered before it resolves, the trigger never happens (419.4.a.1). Triggered abilities that check "play" mean "resolve"; non-triggered checks (like Battering Ram's cost reduction) mean "finalize."

answer:
Yes — playing a card from hand to your Base is playing it, and it will trigger "when you play me."

A card is considered "played" when it completes the entire play process and resolves onto the board (CR 420.4.a) — moving it to the chain, paying costs, and finalizing. That's why the trigger fires after the unit is already on the board, and why your opponent can react to the trigger but not to the unit entering play (FAQ #5735).

Ways that count as "playing" a card:

Normal play from hand — to your Base or a battlefield you control (your exact case).

Playing from other zones — your Chosen Champion zone (CR 420.1.a), or from your trash via abilities like Legion (e.g., Undying Legion).

Effects that play cards for you — e.g., Here to Help ("you may play a unit…"), Hidden spells like Guards!, or token-producing effects. Token units count as "playing a unit" too (Rules 182.1.a, 350.2).

Flipping a Hidden card face-up — that's a play and triggers it; hiding the card face-down does not count as playing it (Rule 737.1.c.1, FAQ #9093).

What does not count: moving a unit already on the board to another battlefield or Base, and being recalled or returned — only the act of playing from a non-board zone triggers it (FAQ #5095). Also, if a spell is countered before resolving, "when you play" effects never trigger (CR 420.4.a.1).

question: If my opponent plays Promising future and from that effect I play Zaun Punk can I wait to see if my opponent plays dazzling aurora to use my zaun punks effect?
answer:

Here's the timing: During Promising Future's resolution, your Zaun Punk goes on the chain first (you're the next player), then the opponent's Dazzling Aurora. Pending items finalize in the order they were added (Rule 337.1.b). Zaun Punk finalizes first and enters play, putting its "when you play me" trigger on the chain as a new pending item. Dazzling Aurora then finalizes and enters play. Only after that does your trigger finalize, at which point you choose the gear to kill (CR 403.2) — and Dazzling Aurora is a legal target.

One catch: the decision to pay the additional cost (kill a friendly gear) must be made when you play Zaun Punk, before you know what the opponent picks. If you pay it up front, you get to choose Dazzling Aurora as the target afterward; if you don't pay it, the trigger never happens.

But Evelynn must be played to the battlefield where she was hidden — your controlled one, not the contested one (Rule 811.1.d.1).

Her trigger says "move an enemy unit at a different location," which is exactly the Tideturner-style exception: because the ability explicitly requires a location that can never be at her own battlefield, she may choose her target freely (CR 811.1.d.3). question: what are some body and mind cards that can help discard your shitty hand and draw another
answer:
Short answer: Body/Mind barely has real "discard a bad hand, draw a new one" filtering — that effect mostly lives in Chaos/Fury. Here's what actually exists in your two domains:

Mind (Blue)

Hwei, Brooding Painter (5E champion) — the only true rummage in Mind: "When I move, draw 1, then discard 1," with a bonus based on what you ditched (Spell → draw 1, Gear → ready 2 runes, Unit → +3 [S]). Pair him with move effects and he's a repeatable filter.

Gutter Palace (4E gear) — discard 1, [T]: play a 1 [S] Bird token with [Deflect]. Turns dead cards into board presence, but no draw.

Pure replacement draw (no discard, but fixes a bricked hand): Progress Day (draw 4), Premonition (draw 3, Reaction), Consult the Past (draw 2, Hidden/Reaction), Renata Glasc, Mastermind ([1] rune: draw 1), Stupefy (draw 1, Reaction).

Body (Orange)

No discard-draw filters exist in Body. Your draw is limited to Spoils of War (draw 2, Reaction, cheaper if an enemy died), Confront (draw 1), Mobilize / Catalyst of Aeons (draw 1 if you couldn't channel), and Qiyana, Victorious (draw 1 on conquer).

If you really want the "pitch hand, draw again" feel, you'll want a Chaos splash, since Mind and Chaos share the Swift Scout legend:

Invert Timelines (Chaos, 3E) — the only true full redraw: "Each player discards their hand, then draws 4."

Traveling Merchant (Chaos, 2E) — discard 1, draw 1 every time it moves (repeatable rummage).

Doran's Ring (Chaos gear) and Zaun Warrens (colorless battlefield) — discard 1, draw 1 on Conquer.

Bottom line: if you're locked to Body/Mind, Hwei plus the big Mind draw spells is your best filter package; actual discard-draw engines need a Chaos splash.

question: !can Tornado Warrior empower something that does not have the empower mechanic? Also, if Tornado Warrior dies after being played from hidden and resolving, does a card that gets empowered still get disempowered at the end of the turn?
answer:
Yes to both.

1. Empowering doesn't require the target to have the Empower keyword or any Empowered ability. Empower is a game action that gives any on-board game object (unit, gear, or legend) the Empowered status — it's a binary state any game object can hold (CR 442.1–442.2). The status does nothing on its own; it only matters if another effect references it. The only restriction is the target can't already be Empowered (CR 442.1.b–c). So Tornado Warrior can empower anything at its battlefield, even a vanilla card.

2. Yes. "Disempower it at end of turn" is a Delayed Trigger created when Tornado Warrior's play-from-hidden ability resolved. Delayed Abilities are not tied to their source's presence — they execute at their specified time regardless of whether the source is still on the board (CR 393). So if Tornado Warrior dies, the disempower still fires at end of turn. One caveat: if the empowered card left the board (it loses Empowered when it leaves) or was already disempowered, the delayed trigger simply does nothing (CR 443.1.a).

Because "you may" is the first part of the effect, the choice whether to perform the ability is made when the trigger finalizes on the Chain (Rule 383.3.a). If you decline, the trigger is removed from the Chain and does nothing — no unit is played.

What you can't do is pick a unit and then skip its cost. Paying the full cost is mandatory as part of playing it (Rule 357); if you can't or won't pay, the play is undone (CR 445.2.a) and the unit just stays in your trash. So the only available "decline" is at the "you may" level — the parenthetical isn't an optional cost.

question: When do you declare to pay the additional cost of cards? what is the order of when the opponent can react
answer:
You declare additional costs as part of playing the card itself, before any reaction window. The choice to pay an optional cost (like Accelerate) is made in Step 2 of the play process, that cost is added to the Total Cost in Step 3 (Rule 356.2), and you pay it — along with base costs and any mandatory "as an additional cost" costs — in Step 4 (Rule 357.1–357.2). The entire play process (declare → choose → pay → legality → finalize) completes before your opponent gets any priority; finalizing doesn't pass priority (Rule 337.1.a).

After the card is finalized, what happens depends on type: a spell stays on the Chain, its controller gets priority first and then priority passes to the opponent in turn order, who may respond with Reactions (only Reactions are legal in a Closed State). If the spell is countered, the costs you already paid are not refunded (CR 426.1.c). Units and Gear instead resolve immediately on finalization (Rule 337.2), so there is no reaction window to the card entering play itself — opponents can only respond to "when you play me" triggers placed on the Chain afterward.

One caveat: costs written inside an effect ("Pay any amount of [A] to deal damage," e.g. Bullet Time) are not play costs — they're paid at resolution, so they don't need to be paid if the card is countered (FAQ #5229).

question: Can I use an action card after a unit has been gusted from the battlefield and there are no more units there?

question: Deck out rules in riftbound
answer:
You can't lose by "decking out" — instead, running out causes a Burn Out, which hands your opponent points.

Drawing the last card is free. As long as your Main Deck has ≥1 card when you draw, you just draw it — no penalty (CR 414.4).

Drawing from an empty deck triggers a Burn Out. You draw as many as possible, shuffle your Trash into your Main Deck (randomized), choose an opponent to gain 1 point, then finish the draw (CR 432.2). If your Trash is also empty, you Burn Out repeatedly — each attempt gives another point.

Burn Out points are dangerous: after the first Burn Out resolves, subsequent points can't be prevented, and if a Burn Out point puts a player at/above the Victory Score, that player wins immediately — no waiting for cleanup (CR 432.3).

Looking/revealing cards doesn't Burn Out — if an effect tells you to reveal/look at the top X but you have fewer, you just reveal as many as possible and resolve it normally (CR 432.1.c).

Milling to Trash (putting cards from deck to Trash) also causes a Burn Out if it exceeds your remaining deck (CR 432.1.b).

question: !ask how does priority during i.e showdown work? I play a reaction spell or unit. Do I still have focus to play another reaction speed unit or spell or does my opponent have it first? Alternatively after resolving the chain, who has priority to i.e open a new chain with an action speed spell?
answer:
Yes to reactions, no to focus. Playing a Reaction (or any chain item) gives you priority first, so you can stack multiple reactions in a row before your opponent gets a chance — focus isn't consumed by reactions (FAQ 4908, Rule 312.2.c/338.1.a.5). You only pass priority when you choose to pass it.

Once the chain empties back to a Showdown Open State, focus passes to the next player in turn order — that player gets priority and may open a new chain with an Action spell (Rule 340.2.a/346). You cannot "hold focus" to chain a second Action; you'd get focus back only after your opponent passes without acting (Rule 347).

One exception: if the chain opened from triggered abilities or an Add ability (e.g., the initial attack/defend trigger chain), focus does not pass when it closes — the attacker keeps it (Rule 346.1, FAQ 8169). Also remember: Actions can only be played during Open State; while the chain is up it's Reactions only.

question: in bf1 attack hahs 1 unit with 5 might. Defence has a Shadow Clone and a Zed, Without a sound. What hahppens in the end of showdown?

Combat Cleanup (CR 468.1): Lethal-damage units are killed (attacker's unit and Zed). Units are then healed, and attackers are only recalled if defenders are still present — but the attacker's unit is already dead, so no recall.

Result (CR 468.3): The Shadow Clone is the only unit remaining, so the defender is the only player with units → defender wins.

Control (CR 468.5): The defender establishes control of the battlefield (clearing Contested), which is a Conquer if they haven't already scored that battlefield this turn.

Note: if the attacker instead split damage (e.g., 1 to the Clone, 4 to Zed), the Clone dies to lethal (1 damage ≥ 0 Might) but Zed survives with 4 damage — defender still wins. The attacker cannot kill both defender units with only 5 damage.

question: Can fortify position give its effect twice? So shield 2 in one combat and then another combat happens to give it shield 2 again so +4
answer:
No. Fortified Position's Shield 2 lasts only "this combat," so the first combat's Shield expires the moment that combat ends (CR 468.7.c). The next combat's trigger gives a fresh Shield 2, but the old one is already gone — the unit ends up with Shield 2 (+2 Might), not Shield 4.

Two things prevent the doubling:

Cross-combat stacking doesn't happen — "this combat" effects all expire simultaneously at the end of combat (CR 468.7.c), so the two grants never coexist.

Fortified Position can't fire twice in one combat either — defend triggers are only checked once per combat (Rule 383.4.f.2.a).

Where Shield does stack is when sources overlap in the same combat — e.g., a unit with native Shield 2 defending on Fortified Position totals Shield 4 (FAQ 2459). But that requires two simultaneous grants, not one per combat.

question: !ask my opponent is asking me to say in plain voice every move I am doing. "I will play..." I want to concentrate on my game and not talk to him. Am I compelled by the rules to do so ? What if I refuse ?
answer:
No — you're not required to narrate every move in plain voice. Rules only require that changes to public information be acknowledged in an "understandable and observable way" — verbally, physically, or by agreed convention — and physically playing a card face-up is itself that acknowledgment (TR 502.6.a). You're also explicitly not required to assist your opponent in playing the game (TR 501.3); the one exception is that scoring points must be verbally announced.

If you refuse: as long as your actions are clear and observable, refusing to narrate is not a violation. However, if your opponent asks a direct question about public information ("what did you just play?"), you must answer honestly — refusing that is a Communication Violation (Warning, TR 703.5/502.7). If they're asking you to read out private/derived info like what a Hidden card is or your hand, you don't have to disclose it. If the demand continues, you can call a judge and keep playing normally in the meantime.

During that Showdown — and since your unit applied the Contested status, you gain Focus first (Rule 345) — you can play the hidden Tideturner as a Reaction. Its errata lets it target a unit you control "at another location" (CR 811.1.d.3), so it swaps with your unit and brings it back; Tideturner takes its place on their battlefield (FAQ 1652, FAQ 281).

Repeat makes the spell's instructions execute a second time (Rule 820.1.d), and each execution is its own "give −[S] to a unit" event. Mel's Empowered ability is a replacement effect that applies to each of those events individually (like the Moonfall ruling, FAQ #11737), turning each −2 into −3. So one cast with Repeat on a single unit = −3, then −3 = −6 Might.

Worth noting: the −6 is treated as 0 Might for game purposes, and this still doesn't kill the unit by itself — it only dies if it has damage marked equal to or greater than its current Might.

question: does mirror image give the unit chosen temporary?
answer:
No — Mirror Image grants Temporary to the Reflection token it creates, not to the unit you chose.

The spell reads "Choose a unit. Play a ready Reflection unit token... It becomes a copy of that unit. Give it [Temporary]." The "it" refers to the Reflection token, so only the copy gets Temporary and is killed at the start of its controller's next Beginning Phase (Rule 816.1.b). The original chosen unit keeps whatever it had and is completely unaffected by the spell. This is also why a Reflection token that fails to copy (e.g. the target left the board) still has Temporary — it comes from the spell's own grant (FAQ #11492).

question: virtuoso, do runes come in ready when you banish 4
answer:
Yes — runes channeled by Virtuoso's ability enter ready.

Runes enter the board ready by default unless the effect explicitly says "channel X runes exhausted" (CR 431.2). Since Virtuoso just says "channel 4 runes," all four come in ready. You can then use them immediately for energy that turn (FAQ #10639).

question: if I have a ruined rex defending against akali silent with 8 might, and I have a karthus at my base, how will this resolve?
answer:
Yes — Karthus makes Ruined Rex's Deathknell fire twice, and both triggers can hit Akali, killing her.

Here's the sequence: Akali (8 Might) and Ruined Rex (6 Might) trade combat damage. Rex takes lethal and dies; Akali takes 6 (non-lethal). Combat Cleanup then heals Akali, and she isn't recalled because no Defenders remain — but she keeps her Attacker designation until Combat ends (CR 468.7). Rex's Deathknell triggers twice since Karthus is on the board (his passive works from Base), creating two separate 4-damage chain items. Those triggers resolve before Combat ends (CR 468.2; FAQ #10444), so Akali is still "in combat" and her "can't be chosen unless in combat" protection does not apply. Both triggers can target her: 4 + 4 = 8 damage equals her Might, so she dies.

question: can you explain all the steps when combat happens, to include deathknell triggers
answer:
Combat only opens through a Cleanup: when opposing units end up at the same Battlefield with no ongoing Combat, the Cleanup stages a Showdown (and a Combat), and the Turn Player picks which Staged Combat to open if there are several (CR 323.6–323.11). From there the sequence is:

1. Combat Showdown Step (CR 466). Attacker (the player who applied Contested) and Defender are designated; Attacker gains Focus. Any triggers generated by that designation go on the Chain (Attacker first, then other players in turn order, Defender last). Players then play cards/abilities with Action or Reaction and pass Focus until all pass — the Showdown closes. If a unit dies here (spell, on-attack trigger), its Deathknell finalizes and resolves now, before any damage.

2. Combat Damage Step (CR 467). If both sides still have units, sum attacker and defender Might. Starting with the Attacker, each player assigns damage equal to their total among the opponent's units — you must assign full lethal to one unit before moving to the next (Tank/Backline reorder this, and some cards redefine "lethal"). Only after all assignment is done is the damage dealt, simultaneously.

3. Resolution Step — Combat Cleanup (CR 468.1, 323). This is where combat-death Deathknells fire:

Units with lethal damage that have Deathknell (or "when I die" abilities) trigger first, as Pending Items, noting their stats/location before they leave (Rule 383.2.c.3).

Those units are then Killed and sent to their owners' trashes (CR 323.4).

All units in play heal (Combat Special Cleanup insertion 3c).

Attackers still present are recalled if defenders remain (3d).

Only after that do the Deathknell triggers finalize and resolve — after healing, so a damaging Deathknell can't finish off survivors (FAQ 10444).

4. After cleanup (CR 468.3–468.7). Determine Combat Result — sole remaining side wins; "No Result" if both or neither have units (which can re-stage Combat). Then establish control, clear Contested, Conquer if you hadn't scored that Battlefield this turn, and remove Attacker/Defender designations as combat ends.

Two gotchas: Deathknell is "when I die", not "when I attack" (Rule 808.1.c), and if the kill is replaced by something like a recall, the Deathknell trigger is removed from the Chain (Rule 808.1.d.1).

question: when do you heal after after combat to include deathknell triggers, breakdown the steps
answer:
Ruling: Deathknell triggers fire before the heal, but they resolve after it — so the heal happens first as far as any play decisions are concerned.

Here's the full combat resolution breakdown (CR 467.3 → 466):

Combat Damage Step (CR 467) — damage is assigned and dealt simultaneously.

FEPR is skipped (CR 467.3) and play jumps straight into the Resolution Step (CR 468.1).

Combat Cleanup begins:

3a (CR 383.2.c.3): Units with lethal damage that have Deathknell (or other "when I die" abilities) trigger just before they are killed — their triggers are processed and placed on the chain, with the information they need noted.

3b (CR 323.5): Those units are Killed and placed in their owner's trash.

3c (CR 468.1.a.1): Heal all units — every unit in play, not just those that fought.

3d (CR 468.1.a.2): Recall attacking units still present if defenders remain.

Determine Combat Result (CR 468.3), then Establish Control / Conquer (CR 468.5) and Combat ends (CR 468.7).

FEPR resumes — only now do the Pending Deathknell triggers get finalized and resolve on the chain.

Practical takeaways: Deathknell cannot finish off units that survived with non-lethal damage (they heal first), and cannot save a unit that took lethal damage (it's already in the trash before anything resolves). Same timing applies to "when I die" abilities — they were aligned with Deathknell in the Vendetta rules update.

FAQ #9514 covers this exact sequence (Rule refs: 465.3, 466.1, 466.1.a.1, 383.2.c.3, 323.5, 808.1.d).

question: Does Astral Herron need to be at a battlefield the moment the first card is played, or only when you want to try to play the next card and use its effects' resources? I.e., I play a card earlier in the turn, resolve it, after which I move my Herron to a contested battlefield and want to use the discount that moment on an action/reaction card. Is this possible?
answer:
No. Heron must already be at a battlefield when your first card of the turn finishes resolving — the "if I'm at a battlefield" check happens at that moment, not later when you want to spend the discount.

The trigger is "When you play your first card each turn, if I'm at a battlefield…" — and that condition is evaluated right after the inciting event (your first card) fully resolves (Rule 383.2.c). If Heron is still in hand/on the board elsewhere at that instant, the conditional fails and the ability never triggers at all. There's no pending discount floating around that you can "activate" later by moving Heron (FAQ #12025).

So in your scenario: play card A, resolve it, then move Heron to a contested battlefield — the discount is gone. You'd have needed Heron at a battlefield before card A resolved. If you want the discount on an action/reaction played later in a showdown, you need to get Heron to a battlefield first and then play your first card of the turn while it's there.

question: If my opponent uses Hard Bargain on my Rampage and I paid the additional cost, do I get the +2 might?
answer:
Yes. If you pay Hard Bargain's [2], Rampage is not countered, and since you already paid Rampage's [C] additional cost when you played it, the +2 Might is granted when Rampage resolves.

Sequence: Hard Bargain resolves first — your [2] payment means its counter effect does nothing. Rampage is still on the Chain, so it resolves normally and your friendly unit gets +2 this turn, then both units deal damage equal to their Mights to each other.

One distinction: Hard Bargain's [2] only stops the counter — it has nothing to do with the +2. The +2 comes only from Rampage's own additional cost ([C] Body), which you pay as you play it (Rule 356–357). If you hadn't paid that, Rampage would still resolve but without the +2.

question: If my opponent plays Spinning Axe into a 3 might unit, can I Gust it in response?
answer:
Yes. Spinning Axe entering the chain opens a Closed State, and since Gust is a [Reaction] you can play it in response — it will resolve first (LIFO) and return the 3 Might unit to its owner's hand. Spinning Axe then resolves, can't attach to the now-gone unit, and enters the battlefield unattached (it'll be killed by its own [Temporary] at your opponent's next Beginning Phase, before scoring).

One caveat: Gust only targets a unit at a battlefield, so this works only if the unit is on a battlefield, not sitting at Base. (RiftJudge FAQ #11482; Chain LIFO, Rule 359.3)

question: Can I play Back Off on my own Irelia Fervent and defy it myself (or abandon or hard bargain, doesn't matter), resulting in the spell not stunning Irelia BUT receiving a +1 from choosing her?
answer:
Yes — Irelia, Fervent keeps the +1, and Back Off gets countered.

When you finalize Back Off and choose Irelia, her "when you choose me" trigger fires immediately and goes on the chain above the spell (the trigger is independent of the spell, so countering it doesn't undo the +1). You can then play Defy (or Abandon/Hard Bargain) targeting your own Back Off — nothing in Defy restricts who controls the spell, and Back Off's 3-energy/0-power cost is within Defy's limit. The chain resolves LIFO: Defy counters Back Off (no stun, and no draw from Back Off's text since it never resolves), then Irelia's trigger gives her +1. Note Deflect doesn't matter here since only opponents pay the extra rune to choose her.

question: When I play a Long Sword or a Sterak's Gage, can I attach it to a unit for free? Or do I have to recycle 1?
answer:
Free on the initial play — no recycle needed.

Both Long Sword and Sterak's Gage have Quick-Draw (Rule 819): "When you play this, attach it to a Unit you control." That triggered ability attaches the gear for free as part of playing it — you only pay the printed Energy/Power cost. The [C] Equip cost (Recycle 1) is only used later, if the gear becomes unattached and you want to reattach it via the normal Equip activated ability (Rule 818).

One note: if you control at least one unit, the Quick-Draw attach is mandatory — you can't play the gear and leave it sitting unattached at your Base.

question: Can you Rebuke a Rengar reaction coming into the battlefield trying to conquer?
answer:
No — not as a reaction to Rengar being played. Rebuke is [Action], not [Reaction], so it can't be added to a chain or played during the Closed State while Rengar's play is resolving (Rules 338.1.a, 813; FAQ #3425).

You do get a window after he resolves: once the chain empties, the showdown reopens and Focus passes to you, and Action spells are playable in showdowns on any turn (Rule 347.1.b; FAQ #8659). So you can play Rebuke then to bounce Rengar back to hand before the showdown closes.

But that alone doesn't stop the Conquer — Rengar's player had to have a unit at that battlefield to be attacking, and if that unit is still there when the showdown closes, they establish control and Conquer anyway (Rule 348.2.a). Rebuke only prevents the Conquer if it leaves them with no units at the battlefield.

question: Me and my opponent play Seat of Power, I conquer with my Lonely Poro and use Shuriken Flip to move it to the other battlefield, do I draw when I conquer?
answer:
No, you don't draw.

Seat of Power's "When you conquer here" trigger goes on the Chain when you conquer. You can absolutely play Shuriken Flip before it resolves and move the Poro to the other battlefield — but moving there only applies Contested to that battlefield. You don't Control it until the resulting Showdown resolves with your units remaining (Rules 190.4 / 466.5), and that resolution happens after your draw trigger has already come off the Chain.

So when the ability resolves, "each other battlefield you or allies control" = 0, and you draw nothing. For the draw to work, you'd need to actually control another battlefield at that moment — winning the Showdown at the other Seat of Power first would conquer it, but that would trigger that battlefield's own draw ability (and you'd have to keep units on the first one or you'd lose control of it in the next Cleanup).

question: When Twilight Reveler moves to an open battlefield does it count as attacking for her ability?
answer:
No. Moving Twilight Reveler to an open battlefield is a non-combat Showdown — she never gains the Attacker designation, so "When I attack" doesn't trigger (FAQ #8664, Rule 383.4.e).

If an opponent later moves a unit into that battlefield during the Showdown, combat begins, she becomes the attacker, and her ability fires then.

question: If I move Akali, Deadly Weapon into a battlefield that my opponent controls with a 1 might tentacle at Threshold of the Gray, the tentacle would die from the Akali move trigger but would my opponent or me add 1 energy as per the battlefield?
answer:
Neither player adds 1 energy — Threshold of the Gray's trigger never fires.

Here's why: Akali's "When I move" trigger resolves and deals 1 (or 2 if Empowered) to the tentacle before Combat is ever staged. In the following Cleanup, the tentacle is killed by that lethal damage, so when the Cleanup checks for opposing units to stage Combat, only Akali remains — that's a Non-Combat Showdown, and Combat never starts. Threshold of the Gray only triggers "when combat starts here" (CR 457–458; FAQ #12145).

If the tentacle had survived, then Combat would start and both players — attacker and defender — would each Add 1, not just one of you.

question: Do I get a token from the yellow Viktor if my Sprite dies?
answer:
Yes — Sprite tokens are Fae units, not Recruits, so when one dies Viktor, Leader creates a 1 Might Recruit token (FAQ #4299; Rule 187.2).

Two caveats: the Sprite has to actually die — if it's bounced to hand (e.g., Gust) it ceases to exist without dying, so no trigger (FAQ #738). And if Viktor dies in the same event as the Sprite, he can't see the death and won't trigger (Rule 383.2.c.2).

question: When I cast Rengar Trophy Hunter on response to the Deathknell of a lonely Poro I had in defense on a battlefield, does my Rengar attack or defend?
answer:
Rengar is the Defender — your opponent remains the Attacker.

Designations are set by Contested status, not by who reacted to what: the player whose unit first applied Contested to that battlefield is the Attacker (CR 461.2.b), and any unit played into a battlefield already Contested by the opponent enters as the Defender. Your Lonely Poro dying doesn't change that — even if it leaves you with no units there, the battlefield is still Contested by the opponent's unit, so Rengar arrives as the Defender and joins (or re-stages) combat on your side. This is the same ruling as the standard "opponent moves in, you ambush Rengar" case (RiftJudge FAQ #9992, #9820).

question: I move in against a Tide Turner with an Empowered Akali deadly weapon. I assign the 2 damage to the Tide Turner. Can my opponent play Star Crossed on both units and save his Tide Turner?
answer:
Yes — if that 2 damage is Akali's Empowered move trigger, your opponent can play Star-Crossed in response and save the Tideturner. Star-Crossed is a [Reaction], so it's playable while your trigger is on the chain. It resolves first (LIFO), returning both units to hand; when your trigger then resolves, Tideturner is in a non-board zone and is no longer a legal target, so the damage instruction is ignored (Rule 359.3.e.5).

One timing caveat: if you mean combat damage has already been assigned — no. Once the Showdown closes and assignment begins, there's no window to play anything (FAQ #10832). Your opponent's last chance was to play Star-Crossed before the Showdown closed, which would also save the Tideturner by removing both units before the damage step.

question: If someone cast a spell on my Master Yi with Repeat, does he have to pay Deflect cost for each repeat?
answer:
Yes — Deflect is a mandatory additional cost applied "for each time they choose me" (Rule 809.1.c), so each targeting instance costs extra.

When your opponent pays a spell's Repeat cost, the spell's instructions (including choosing targets) are executed an additional time, and those choices are made when the spell is played (Rule 820.2). So if the spell chooses Master Yi for both the initial and the repeated execution, they must pay the Deflect cost twice — and if they can't, they can't make that choice. This assumes Master Yi, Tempered at Level 6+ (the version with Deflect); Master Yi, Unstoppable can't be chosen at all at Level 16.

question: Does Public Execution target the enemy unit on cast or resolution?
answer:
On cast. Public Execution chooses (targets) both the friendly unit and the enemy unit when it's finalized onto the chain — not on resolution.

"Choose a friendly unit" targets the friendly unit, and "Kill an enemy unit with less Might than it" targets the enemy unit, with "with less Might than it" acting as a targeting restriction (Rule 355.10). You must have a legal enemy unit — one with Might strictly less than your friendly unit's current Might — before you can even play the spell.

If the Might math changes before it resolves (your friendly unit loses Might, or the enemy gains Might so it's no longer "less"), the enemy target is no longer legal and is simply unaffected when the spell resolves — you can't swap to a different unit.

question: If I'm holding 2 locations and I put Tide Turner hidden on location B and then it's the enemy turn and they contest Battlefield A, can I Tide Turner reveal location B and swap my Battlefield A and B unite?
answer:
Yes — you can. Playing a hidden Tideturner from Battlefield B to swap with your unit at Battlefield A during the opponent's Showdown at A is fully legal.

Here's how it works: Tideturner played from hidden has Reaction, so you get a window to play it during the Showdown at A — either by responding to something on the Chain (the attack trigger, an action-speed effect) or when the opponent passes priority to you. Its errata'd "When you play me" trigger lets it target a unit you control at any location, bypassing the normal hidden targeting restriction (FAQ 11326).

When it resolves, Tideturner moves to A and your unit moves back to B. Since B is a battlefield you control, no new Contested is applied there, and A is already Contested by the opponent — the Combat at A simply continues with Tideturner as your unit. The swap happens as one uninterrupted resolution, so you can't lose control of A mid-swap.

question: Does Flurry of Blades work on Barron?
answer:
Yes — Flurry of Blades hits Baron Nashor, though it won't kill him on its own.

Flurry of Blades doesn't target or "choose" units; it programmatically affects all units at battlefields (Rule 352.10.d, FAQ #1583). Baron's protection only stops enemy spells/abilities from choosing him, so the 1 damage applies. Since Baron has 12 Might, he just takes 1 damage and survives unless the damage is lethal-modified (e.g., you control Elder Dragon).

question: Would a Flurry of Blades and Elder Dragon in the enemy base kill my Baron?
answer:
Yes — your Baron dies.

Flurry of Blades deals 1 to all units at battlefields without choosing any targets, so Baron Nashor's "I can't be chosen by enemy spells and abilities" doesn't protect him — that protection only stops spells/abilities that choose or target him. Since your opponent controls Elder Dragon, that 1 damage is "their damage," and their passive makes any amount of it lethal to enemy units. Baron takes the damage and is killed in the following cleanup; Elder Dragon being in base (rather than at a battlefield) doesn't matter.

The only way Baron survives is if the damage is prevented (e.g., Unyielding Spirit) — otherwise 1 damage is enough to kill him. (RiftJudge FAQ #8684/#10171; CR 323.4.)

question: Back Off being defy, has the card count been played or not? For the effect "if you played this from your hand, draw 1".
answer:
No — you don't draw. A countered spell is removed from the chain without resolving, so none of Back Off's instructions are carried out — including "If you played this from your hand, draw 1."

This matches how Defy works against any spell: countering means the card never resolves (CR 426.1.a), and a countered card is also not considered "played" for effects that check that (CR 426.1.b). So even the "played from your hand" condition isn't satisfied — Back Off goes straight to your trash and you get neither the Stun nor the draw.

question: Are targets chosen for Cull the Weak when it is put on the stack or when it resolves?
answer: No — Cull the Weak never targets. Its text "Each player kills one of their units" falls under Rule 355.10.e, so each player independently chooses a unit as the spell resolves, not when it's put on the chain. Nothing is locked in at play, and you can even cast it with an empty board — if you have no units at resolution, you just don't kill one (do as much as you can). Because it doesn't target, it also bypasses Deflect and cards like Not So Fast that require targeting.

question: How does winning combat constitute? Is it conquering or killing one unit?
answer:
Neither — you win a combat by being the only player with units remaining at that battlefield when the Combat Result is determined (CR 468.3.a).

No kills required: the opponent's units can die, get bounced, or be moved away — if only your units remain, you win the combat. No damage needs to have been dealt at all. Conversely, killing all their units is meaningless if you don't have any units left yourself — that's "No Result," not a win (CR 468.3.d).

Conquering is a separate thing that follows winning: after the result, the player with units remaining establishes control, and that's what triggers a Conquer point if they haven't scored that battlefield yet (CR 468.5.d). You can also Conquer with no combat at all (moving onto an empty battlefield) — that's a Non-Combat Showdown, and it is not winning a combat.

question: If I move red Akali to a battlefield where my enemy has a 1 might unit, my ability does 1 damage to his unit when I move to this battlefield, does my opponent can play a card action/reaction, or does it instantly die?
answer:
They can play Reactions, but not Actions — and if they don't react, the 1-Might unit dies before any Action window opens.

When Akali, Deadly Weapon moves, her "When I move" trigger goes on the Chain immediately, putting the game in a Closed State (Rule 354.1). In that state your opponent may only play cards/abilities with Reaction — Action spells can't be played because no Showdown is staged yet. So they can save the unit with a Reaction (moving it to base, preventing the damage, buffing its Might, etc.), but if they pass, her trigger resolves dealing 1 damage and kills the 1-Might unit on the spot.

Only after that chain empties and a Cleanup runs does the Showdown officially begin (FAQ #11684, #12081). Your opponent's first chance to play an Action comes inside the Showdown once it opens — and since you applied Contested, you get Focus first (Rule 345). By then the damage has already resolved, so without a Reaction the unit is gone.

question: Can you have a hidden card on a battlefield with no other cards?
answer:
Yes — but only temporarily, and only if you controlled that battlefield first.

You can't hide a card at a battlefield with no units to begin with: Hiding requires a Battlefield you control (Rule 811.1.b), and control is established by having units there (Rule 190.4). So the hidden card always starts alongside at least one unit.

Once it's there, if all your units leave or die, what happens depends on the game state:

During an ongoing Showdown/Combat at that battlefield: you keep control, the hidden card stays, and you can still play it even with no units present (FAQ #6143).

Outside of combat (Open State): you lose control of the battlefield in the following cleanup if you have no units there (Rule 190.4.c), and the hidden card is removed to your trash.

So a lone hidden card on an empty battlefield can exist, but it's a temporary state — it survives only through combat, then goes away.

question: On Jayce Ready trigger, can I place a Trinity Force on a unit at a battlefield if I have in base "Jax Unmatched" to double hold?
answer:
Yes. You can play Trinity Force from hand as a Reaction on Jayce's ready trigger (a Closed State) and attach it to a unit at a battlefield, and the unit will then double-hold.

Jax, Unmatched grants all your Equipment Quick-Draw "everywhere," so Trinity Force has [Reaction] plus "When you play it, attach it to a unit you control." Quick-Draw's auto-attach has no location restriction — the gear's location simply becomes the unit's (CR 435.4), and gear attached to a unit at a battlefield is legal (Rule 152.2). Pay only the play cost; the attach is free (FAQ #1989).

Once attached, Trinity Force's effect text ("When I hold, score 1 point") is appended to the unit's rules text (CR 435.1.c). So when that unit holds, you score the battlefield's hold point plus Trinity Force's point — and the unit's own hold trigger still fires too.

Two notes: play it from hand (Quick-Draw doesn't attach gear already on the board, and you can't use Equip at Reaction speed — FAQs #10839, #9085), and make sure the attachment happens before the Beginning Phase hold. Jayce's trigger itself is unaffected — it's just your timing window.

question: Diana on Ravenbloom Conservatory. What triggers first, the when I defend or the when a showdown begins?
answer:
Diana's "When a showdown begins here" triggers first. Ravenbloom Conservatory's "When you defend here" is a Defend Trigger that only fires once the Defender designation is assigned — and that happens after the showdown begins.

Order of events when the opponent moves in and Combat opens (CR 466.2):

Showdown begins — Task 1 "Start of combat or showdown effects happen now" → Diana triggers (Rule 466.2.b).

Task 2 establishes Attacker/Defender → you gain the Defender designation → Ravenbloom triggers (CR 466.2.c, 383.4.f).

One practical nuance: both go on the Combat Chain in Task 4, with the Defender's triggers placed last (CR 466.2.d.1). Since Diana's became pending first, Ravenbloom's sits on top of it — so on resolution (LIFO), Ravenbloom's reveal resolves before Diana's Predict/draw. And if the Showdown were non-Combat (no enemy unit present), you'd never get the defend trigger at all (Rule 383.4.f).

question: If enemy held at battlefield A, moved his unit to battlefield B, then they used another unit to move to battlefield A again, can I react to that?
answer:
Yes — you get a window to act, but not directly in response to the move itself. A Standard Move never opens a chain (CR 442.3), so you can't play a Reaction "on" the move as it happens.

However, once the enemy moved their unit out of A, they lost control of it in the following cleanup, so their second unit moving into A applies Contested and stages a Non-Combat Showdown. During that showdown the enemy has Focus first, but when they pass — or after any chain they start resolves — Focus passes around, and you can play Action or Reaction cards (e.g., kill or bounce their unit) before it re-establishes control. They won't re-score A this turn since it was already scored, but the interference window is still there. If the moving unit has a "when I move" trigger, that trigger also opens a chain you can react to (FAQ #3218).

question: If you cast a card that swaps position from Astral Heron like Resonating Strike to move him to a battlefield, do you get his trigger as the first spell would be Resonating Strike?
answer:
Yes. The "if I'm at a battlefield" check happens after your first card fully resolves (Rule 383.2.c), and Resonating Strike's move happens during that resolution — so when the condition is evaluated, Heron is already at the battlefield and the trigger fires. Your next card that turn costs [2][A][A] less.

This is the mirror of the Retreat case (FAQ #12025): moving Heron off the board before the check fails the trigger; moving him onto a battlefield as part of the first card's resolution satisfies it. Note Resonating Strike being a [Reaction] spell doesn't matter — it's still your "first card each turn" regardless of when you play it.

question: Does Leblanc reflection copy equipped gear as well?
answer:
No. The Reflection copies only the unit's "copyable traits" (printed Might and Rules Text) — Gear is a separate object attached to the unit, so it does not carry over (FAQ #11044).

That means no Equipment, its Might bonus, or its granted effects come with the copy. Buffs and other appended/granted modifications also don't transfer, per the copy-effect rules (Patch Notes 2026-03-30). The original keeps its gear; the Reflection enters as a clean copy.

question: If Shady Spectacles is on a recruit token unit and it is copying a 4 might card, then conquers and Leblanc makes a reflection. Is the reflection a 1 might recruit or a 4 might other card?
answer:
The Reflection is a copy of the 4-Might card, not a 1-Might Recruit.

Shady Spectacles makes the equipped Recruit token become a copy of the 4-Might card, and once a copy effect applies, the copied traits become the unit's new copyable traits ("If you copy a copy, the new copy becomes a copy of the originally copied object"). So at the moment the Recruit conquers, its copyable traits are the 4-Might card's — name, type, Might, rules text — not "1 [M] Recruit."

When Deceiver plays the Reflection and it becomes a copy of "another unit there" (the equipped Recruit), it copies that unit's copyable traits, which are the 4-Might card's. It does not copy the Shady Spectacles gear itself (gear is a separate attached object, not a trait), nor any buffs — but it inherits the full copied identity of the 4-Might card.

Ruling: The Reflection enters as a 4-Might copy of the 4-Might card. (Copy effects — CR 474.1.b.3; Patch Notes 2026-03-30 copyable-traits rule.)

question: Can the purple vex stun Nash?
answer:
Yes. Vex, Apathetic's ability stuns Baron Nashor because "Stun it" programmatically selects the unit that triggered the ability — it's not a choice, so it never targets. Baron's "can't be chosen by enemy spells and abilities" only blocks targeting effects (Rule 355.10.c, 355.10.d; FAQ #8685).

Sequence: your opponent plays Baron → Vex's "When an opponent plays a unit" trigger goes on the chain → it resolves and stuns Baron, also locking it from moving that turn. Contrast: an ability that says "choose/stun an enemy unit" (like Vi, Peacekeeper's) would fail against Baron, because that's a real choice and thus a target (FAQ #10502).

question: Can you equip an equipped equipment? Like a Spinning Axe, can I change its target?
answer:
No. While Spinning Axe is attached to a unit, its Equip ability is inactive — attached cards' printed rules text is turned off — so you can't pay [A] to re-target it (Rule 718.2; FAQ #6999).

To "change its target," the gear has to be detached first: if its unit is killed or recalled, Spinning Axe detaches, returns to your Base ready, and you can Equip it to another unit. Effects that let you move already-attached gear (Weaponmaster, Jax's Legend, etc.) explicitly say so — plain Equip doesn't.

question: If I Temporal Breach a unit that's equipped, what happens?
answer:
The equipment detaches and the unit comes back unequipped.

When Temporal Breach banishes the equipped unit, the unit moves from a board zone to a non-board zone (Banishment), which breaks the attachment — the gear detaches and stays at the unit's last location (CR 436.4.b). The unit is then played back to that same location, ignoring its cost, as a fresh game object: no equipment, no buffs, no damage (FAQ #11709). If the unit was at a Battlefield when banished, the now-unattached gear will be Recalled to its controller's Base at the next Cleanup (CR 436.4.a, 459.1). One caveat: if the unit was a token, it ceases to exist in Banishment and never returns (FAQ #11668).

question: If I gust a star crossed enemy unit while it's targeting my unit, does star cross fizzle?
answer:
No — Star-Crossed doesn't fizzle; it still resolves and returns your unit.

You Gust the enemy unit that Star-Crossed is targeting. Gust resolves first, returning that unit to hand. Since that unit has now moved to a non-board zone, it's no longer the same game object, so Star-Crossed's instruction for it is ignored (Rule 359.3.e.8). But your unit remains a valid target, so Star-Crossed still resolves and returns your unit to your hand.

There's no "fizzle" in Riftbound — spells resolve as much as possible, ignoring only instructions tied to illegal targets. Your only way out would have been to make your own unit illegal (e.g., moving it to a non-board zone) before Star-Crossed resolved. (FAQ #11166)

question: What happens if my Fizz, which is the target for my Star Crossed, gets removed from board at Reaction speed prior to Star Crossed completion? Does the spell activate anyway and my opponent's unit goes to hand?
answer:
Yes — the enemy unit still goes to hand. Star-Crossed doesn't fizzle when one target is removed; it resolves as much as possible and only the instruction affecting the now-invalid target is ignored (Rule 359.3.e.5, 359.3.e.8; FAQ #10311, #10736).

So if Fizz is recalled, killed, or otherwise leaves the board before Star-Crossed resolves, the friendly half of the instruction is ignored — but the enemy unit remains a valid target and is still returned to its owner's hand. The only way the whole spell fails is if both targets are gone.

question: If I ambush a unit on Starspring and try to trigger it, but that unit gets gusted, can I play that unit again and still trigger Starspring?
answer:
No. Star Spring triggers only "the first time a player plays a non-token unit here each turn," and that first-time trigger is already used up for you this turn — Gusting your ambush unit doesn't reset it.

The Gust also doesn't cancel the trigger that's already on the chain: Star Spring's ability resolves on its own to move another unit you control there to base, even if the unit that triggered it was bounced. Replaying that unit to Star Spring is a second play by you this turn, so the ability won't trigger again (Rule 383.3.e.1).

One caveat: if instead of performing the trigger you had declined it during finalization (the "you may"), it's considered to have not triggered, and a later play of a non-token unit there could trigger it (Rule 383.3.e.2.b).

question: If I had 2 otterpus on turn 2 that conquered, do I draw 2 cards instead of one?
answer:
No — you draw 1 card, not 2.

Otterpus's ability is a replacement effect ("would score 1 point... draw 1 instead"), and Rule 370.2 states a replacement effect can only be applied once to an event or to the events that replace it. When your first Otterpus replaces the scoring event with "draw 1," that draw is no longer a scoring event, so the second Otterpus has nothing to replace — the two copies don't stack. If you control two Otterpus, you choose which one applies (Rule 372), but the result is the same: one draw instead of one point.

question: If you play Brynhir Thundersong on Frozen Fortress, then trigger Temporal Breach on your opponent's turn, does it get to play runes that turn?
answer:
Yes — the opponent still channels and uses their runes that turn. Brynhir only stops "playing cards"; channeling (CR 431) is a game action, and rune abilities like "Add [1]" or "Recycle: Add [C]" are activations, not card plays — same logic as Brynhir not stopping gear abilities already on board (FAQ #8627).

Note the timing: her "When you play me" lockdown only covers "this turn," so replaying her via Temporal Breach on the opponent's turn locks down the rest of that turn — they can't play cards from hand or Hidden (including revealing Hidden cards), but runes and board abilities keep working. And since the opponent's Channel Phase happens at the start of their turn, they'll have already channeled their 2 runes before the lockdown even lands.

question: Can I revive Gust Monk by empowering Matriarch without having to spend the extra energy?
answer:
Yes — you can play Gust Monk off Tail-Cloaked Matriarch's Empower trigger without paying the extra [1].

"Play it to your base, ignoring its cost" only zeroes the base Energy and Power costs (Rule 356.1.b). Gust Monk's "[1] as an additional cost" is an optional additional cost — "may pay" — so you can simply decline it (Rule 356.2.b). He still qualifies as a target since his printed cost is 2 Energy / 0 Power (within Matriarch's 3 / 1 limit, per FAQ #6562's printed-cost precedent).

The only catch: if you skip the [1], you won't get the "banish a card from any trash to give Assault 2" effect — that only happens if you actually paid the additional cost. If you'd rather have that effect, you may choose to pay the [1] even while the base cost is ignored.

question: If I played Bellows Breath on a Stellacorn and then after that resolves I play a Thousand Tail, will the Stellacorn die?
answer:
Yes, the Stellacorn dies.

Here's why: damage is "marked" on a unit and doesn't reduce its Might. Bellows Breath leaves 1 damage on the Stellacorn Herder (3 Might — not enough to kill it). Then Thousand-Tailed Watcher's "when you play me" trigger resolves, giving enemy units −3 Might this turn (minimum 1), dropping the Herder to 1 Might. Since the 1 marked damage now equals its Might, it's killed in the following state check.

If you paid the [Repeat] cost on Bellows Breath, the Herder would have 2 damage marked and die just the same. Either way, the −3 Might is what makes the earlier damage lethal.

question: On Falling Star, when you say deal 3 to a unit, does it remove the full 3 might, or just the HP part of the unit?
answer:
It just marks 3 damage — it doesn't touch the unit's Might at all.

In Riftbound, "dealing 3" puts 3 damage counters on the unit (CR 418.1.b). Might and damage are tracked separately: a unit's Might stays at whatever its current modified value is, and damage just sits on it as a marker of how close it is to dying. The unit only actually dies during a Cleanup if its marked damage equals or exceeds its Might (CR 142.4, 323.4).

So a 6-Might unit hit by one instance of Falling Star has 6 Might and 3 damage marked — it keeps all 6 Might. It won't die from that alone; you'd need to either deal 3 more damage or later reduce its Might below its marked damage (e.g., with a -Might effect). And note damage heals at end of turn or Combat Cleanup, so the "3 HP missing" state only persists until then.

question: Can you play a reaction spell to Elder Dragons ability?
answer:
Yes. Elder Dragon's "When you play me" ability is a triggered ability that goes on the Chain, which creates a Closed State — so you can play a [Reaction] spell targeting that ability.

Note the nuance: you can't react to Elder Dragon itself being played (units resolve immediately and never linger on the Chain — FAQ 5909), but its play trigger is a separate Chain item and is fully reactable (FAQ 4606, 9377). One more caveat: its passive ability ("Any amount of your damage is enough to kill enemy units") is not on the Chain and can't be countered — only the triggered damage ability can.

question: If enemy Elder Dragon targets a unit at each battlefield and then I react with Tideturner to swap my units, does Elder Dragon still kill the targeted unit I moved?
answer:
No — your units live.

Tideturner's trigger resolves first (LIFO), so by the time Elder Dragon's play effect resolves, each originally targeted unit is at a different location than the one it was chosen at. Elder Dragon's ability is a series of per-location restrictions ("deal 1 to up to one enemy unit at battlefield A, ... at battlefield B, ..."), and those choices are locked in at finalization. A unit that left its chosen location no longer fulfills that restriction, so the instruction affecting it is ignored — it takes no damage (Rules 359.3.e.5, 359.3.e.9; see FAQ #10312, same principle as Flash vs. Elder Dragon in FAQ #9919). Its lethal-damage passive never comes into play because the damage is never dealt.

question: I have a hidden Pyke and one other unit, opponent uses Falling Star on the other unit, I react with the Pyke, can they choose Pyke after it has revealed or does their choice stick?
answer:
No — their choice sticks. Falling Star's targets are locked in when it's placed on the chain; revealing Pyke doesn't give them a new choice.

When your opponent plays Falling Star, they choose both "Deal 3 to a unit" targets at finalization (Rule 355.5/355.6). Per Rule 355.15, those choices can't be changed afterward unless a spell or ability says otherwise — and your hidden Pyke wasn't even a legal target at that point, since a facedown hidden card isn't a unit on the board. When Falling Star resolves, it deals its 3 (or 6, if both instances chose the same unit) to the original target, and your freshly revealed Pyke is untouched.

The reveal itself is legal (a hidden card gains [Reaction] while facedown, Rule 811.6), it just doesn't affect who Falling Star is pointing at.

question: Can I use Punch First when enemy use Rampage on me?
answer:
No. Punch First is an [Action] spell, so it can only be played when the Chain is empty (Open State) — while Rampage is on the Chain, the game is in a Closed State and only [Reaction] cards can be played (Rule 334.1.a.1).

Rampage resolves first and the damage is dealt before you'd ever get an Open State window to play Punch First. So you can't use it to save your unit or pump it before the damage lands. Your only responses to Rampage are Reaction-speed cards (or abilities with Reaction).

question: I have combined 4 Might as a Rengar player and I want to play Kinkou Initiate. Can I draw a card with using Rengar ability or is this ability after I played a card?
answer:
Yes, you can draw. Both abilities trigger at the same time ("When you play a unit" / "When you play me"), and since you control both, you choose the order they go on the chain (Rule 333.1).

Put Kinkou Initiate's draw trigger on the chain first, then Pridestalker's +1 Might on top. The chain resolves top-down, so Rengar's buff lands first — bumping one of your other units to push their total to 5 — and then Kinkou Initiate resolves and checks "your other units have total Might 5 or more" at that moment. That check happens on resolution, not when the card was played, so the buff counts and you draw 1.

Note Kinkou Initiate checks your other units only — its own 3 Might doesn't count toward the 5.

question: If two Ekkos die at the same time, am I able to resolve one, float all my runes energy, then ready again off the second?
answer:
Yes — two Ekkos dying at once means two separate Deathknell triggers, so you can do the "double-dip" twice.

Both triggers go on the Chain (you choose their order), and they resolve one at a time. First trigger resolves: recycle that Ekko, ready all runes. With the second trigger still on the Chain, you control the newest item and have priority, so you can exhaust all your runes at Reaction speed to float energy. Then the second trigger resolves: recycle the other Ekko, ready all runes again. Since each Ekko is a separate game object, you can recycle both — the "can't recycle the same card twice" limit from FAQ #7490 doesn't apply here. You end with all your runes ready and double-floated energy in your pool until end of turn (Rule 167).

question: Can you reveal a hidden Zhonyas at a battlefield to prevent a unit at base from dying from Public Execution?
answer:
Yes. A hidden Zhonya's Hourglass at a battlefield can be revealed in reaction to Public Execution to save a friendly unit at base from dying.

Public Execution is a spell on the chain, so you have a window to react before it resolves. A hidden card gains Reaction while facedown (Rule 811.1.b), so you can play it for [0] at that time. Zhonya's replacement effect doesn't target a unit and isn't a play ability, so the Hidden targeting restriction that would limit it to its own battlefield never applies — it saves the next friendly unit that would die anywhere, including base (FAQ #1806). And if the saved unit is already at base, the "recall it" instruction is simply ignored; the death is still replaced (FAQ #7310).

One catch: if the unit dying is your only unit on that battlefield, don't wait past the cleanup — once you lose control of the battlefield, the hidden Zhonya's gets trashed (Rule 107.3.d). Reveal it while the spell is still on the chain.

question: Does Confront and Haven's Bar work together ?
answer: No - because the units enter ready, they won't "become ready", and thus won't trigger Pirate's Haven.

question: If Heedless Resurrection is used during combat on the enemy turn can I play the new card to a battlefield during combat
answer:
Yes, you can play the resurrected unit to the battlefield where the combat is taking place. According to RiftJudge FAQ #11033, the process works as follows:

Sequence of Events

Reaction: As a defender during combat, you play Heedless Resurrection as a [Reaction]. This opens a chain and sets the game state to Closed.

Cost: You kill a friendly unit at the battlefield to pay the additional cost. Although you may have removed your only unit there, you do not lose control of the battlefield because the game state is Closed while the spell is on the chain (Rule 187.4.c).

Resolution: Heedless Resurrection resolves. Because you still retain control of the battlefield, it remains a valid destination for the unit you are playing from your trash.

Entry: Once played, the new unit enters the battlefield. If the combat (showdown) is still ongoing, it will participate as a defender (CR 461.2.b.4.a).

Important Constraints

Targeting and Costs: You must follow standard targeting and cost rules: the unit you resurrect must be in your trash before you play Heedless Resurrection, and you cannot retroactively resurrect the unit you just killed to pay the cost (FAQ #9523, #11554).

Cost Requirement: The resurrected unit must have an Energy and Power cost no greater than the unit you killed.

This interpretation is based on Rule 187.4.c and RiftJudge FAQ #11033.

Note: I could not fully verify the citation of Rule 357.2 regarding the cost constraint against the retrieved rules.

question: Does decree of focus give +4 if i thrill of the hunt the fury unit to another battlefield.
answer:
No, Decree of Focus will not grant +4 Might in this scenario.

Reasoning

"New Object" Rule: According to Rule 359.3.e.4 and FAQ #9870, when Thrill of the Hunt banishes a unit and then plays it back to a battlefield, that unit is removed from play and re-enters as a new game object.

Severing Targeting Relationships: When a unit becomes a "new object," any existing targeting relationships or active modifiers tied to its previous state (as the "original" object) are severed.

Decree of Focus Requirement: Decree of Focus requires you to choose a unit "in combat with an enemy Fury unit." While Thrill of the Hunt moves the unit, the re-entered unit is a new object. Even if you were to cast Decree of Focus in response to the Thrill of the Hunt (to target the unit before it leaves the board), that effect would effectively fizzle or be removed because the unit it was targeting has changed into a new game object. If you attempt to play Decree of Focus after the unit has re-entered, the check for whether it is "in combat" will be evaluated based on the new battlefield situation, but the +4 Might will not persist from any previous state.

Summary: Because the unit becomes a new game object when moved by Thrill of the Hunt, it loses all previous modifiers and targeting relationships. You cannot use these cards to maintain or transfer a +4 Might buff in this way.

Note: I could not fully verify this ruling against the retrieved rules.

question: I play decree of focus in a showdown against a body and fury unit. Opponent plays thrill of the hunt and targets the fury unit and places it on another battlefield. Will my unit get +4 might?
answer:
No, your unit will not get +4 Might.

Sequence of Events

Play: You play Decree of Focus targeting a friendly unit at a battlefield occupied by an enemy Fury unit. It is placed on the chain.

Reaction: Your opponent plays Thrill of the Hunt in response, targeting their Fury unit. It is placed on the chain on top of your Decree of Focus.

Resolution – Thrill of the Hunt: Thrill of the Hunt resolves first. It banishes the target Fury unit, and then its owner plays it to a different battlefield.

Object Change: According to CR 705 and RiftJudge FAQ #9870, when a unit is banished and then re-played, it enters the board as a "new object."

Resolution – Decree of Focus: Now it is time for your Decree of Focus to resolve.

The requirement for Decree of Focus is that your unit must be "in combat with an enemy Fury unit" or "being chosen by an enemy Fury spell."

Because the Fury unit moved to a new battlefield, the specific Fury unit that justified your targeting of the Decree of Focus is no longer present at your battlefield.

Per the rules governing mistargeting and condition checks (Rule 359.3.e), because the conditions of the spell are no longer satisfied, the effect fails to apply.

Summary: Since the Fury unit left your battlefield, your unit is no longer in combat with a Fury unit, and the Decree of Focus fails to provide the +4 Might.

Note: I could not fully verify this ruling against the retrieved rules.
