question: My oponent has a crab and a Ferrous Forerunner. If I attack with 6 might, I can kill both, or I need 7 might to assign 1 in crab?
answer:
To address your question about combat damage assignment, we must first look at the stats of your opponent's units:

Ferrous Forerunner: 6 Might

Scuttle Crab: 0 Might

1. The Minimum Lethal Requirement

As established in FAQ #10658, 0-Might units do not die just by existing. They require 1 point of damage to be marked on them to be considered lethally damaged and killed.

2. Can you kill both with 6 Might?

No, you cannot kill both with 6 Might.

According to CR 467.2.c.3 and FAQ #1675, you must assign lethal damage to a unit before moving to the next.

Targeting the Forerunner: You assign 6 damage to the Ferrous Forerunner. This is its exact Might, which constitutes lethal damage.

Targeting the Crab: Since you have already assigned lethal damage to the Ferrous Forerunner, you have fulfilled the requirement to move on to the next unit, but you have 0 Might remaining to assign to the Scuttle Crab.

Crucially: You are not required to kill every unit on the battlefield to win combat; however, you only conquer the battlefield if the enemy has no units remaining after the Combat Damage step.

If you assign all 6 damage to the Ferrous Forerunner, it will be killed.

The Scuttle Crab (with 0 damage marked) will remain on the battlefield.

Result: You have not cleared the battlefield; therefore, your units will be recalled to your base during the Combat Cleanup.

Summary

To kill the Ferrous Forerunner: You must assign at least 6 damage.

To kill the Scuttle Crab: You must assign at least 1 damage.

Total needed to kill both: You need 7 Might (6 for the Forerunner + 1 for the Crab).

With 6 Might, you can successfully kill the Ferrous Forerunner, but you will not have the remaining damage pool necessary to kill the Scuttle Crab, meaning the Scuttle Crab will survive and you will not win the battlefield.

question: can purple mel activate empower without a target enemy unit
answer:
Yes, you can activate the Empower ability on Mel, Newly Awakened without a target enemy unit.

According to Rule 827.1.c.1 and Rule 827.1.b.1, the Empower keyword is an activated ability that specifically targets or requires no units to be on the board. The cost to activate Mel's Empower ability is simply [3], and the effect of that ability is only to make Mel "Empowered."

The text on Mel that references giving units -[M] is an Empowered ability (Rule 828.1.b), which is a separate, dependent effect that only becomes active after Mel has already become Empowered. Activating the Empower keyword does not require any targets; it only requires that Mel is not already Empowered.

The second part of the ability—"When I become [Empowered], banish an enemy unit at a battlefield with 3 [M] or less"—is a triggered ability that occurs after Mel becomes Empowered. If there is no legal target available when that ability resolves, the instruction will simply fail to find a target and nothing else will happen (as per Rule 359.3.e.6).

question: In a Competitive OPL event, how many cards is a player required to bring? & sideboard

In a Competitive OPL Constructed event, your deck registration must consist of the following:

question: If someone plays the harrowing does he target something and puts it on the chain? If so can I disposal order that card before it resolves?
answer:
Yes, you can use Disposal Order to prevent a unit from being played by The Harrowing.

Here is how the interaction works:

The Harrowing is played

The Harrowing becomes a pending chain item, the game state becomes Closed, and The Harrowing goes through the process of finalization (unless something prevents this). When your opponent finalizes The Harrowing, they must choose a unit in their trash as a target. Because the spell's instructions require choosing a specific game object (the unit in the trash), that unit is targeted when The Harrowing is finalized on the chain.

You react with Disposal Order

Because Disposal Order has the Reaction keyword, you can play it while The Harrowing is still on the chain waiting to resolve.
You play Disposal Order and choose the unit your opponent targeted with The Harrowing (and up to two other cards) from their trash.
These cards are then recycled to the bottom of their owner's deck.

Resolution

The chain resolves in reverse order (LIFO). Disposal Order resolves first, and those cards are moved to the deck.
Next, The Harrowing attempts to resolve. Because the unit it was targeting is no longer in the trash (it has changed zones to the deck), the target is now illegal.
Per Rule 359.3.e.1, the spell resolves anyway, but because its instruction cannot be executed (there is no valid unit to play), it has no effect on the board.

Summary: By reacting to The Harrowing with Disposal Order, you move the intended unit out of the trash before The Harrowing can pull it into play, effectively countering the spell's primary effect.

question: how does glowstone interaction work, can enemies do anything
answer:
Glowstone is a hot potato — whoever controls it at the end of their own turn eats it: Glowstone kills itself and deals 5 damage to all units that player controls. Enemies have several ways to interact.

The loop: play it to your Base, pay [A][A] to Empower it, then activate "Disempower this, [T]" to hand it to an opponent — it's recalled to their Base (still exhausted, no longer empowered). At the start of their Ending Step (Rule 317.1) its trigger fires, and in the following cleanup all their units with Might 5 or less die; Might 6+ survive and heal (CR 323.4.3b + 317.2.b–c). It hits units at Bases and Battlefields alike.

What the enemy can do:

Remove it — it's a targetable Gear at their Base (Rule 148.1.a.3). Kill/bounce it in their Main Phase before their Ending Step and the trigger never fires. They can even respond to the pass ability itself with a Reaction spell; if Glowstone is gone when it resolves, the hand-off fails.

Pass it back — on their Main Phase they can pay [A][A] to re-Empower it, then use its own ability to hand it to you (or a third player), who then takes the 5 at the end of their turn. They can't use the ability on a non-empowered Glowstone — "Disempower this" isn't payable when it isn't empowered (CR 443.1.a.1, 203.3) — so they must empower first.

Once the trigger is on the Chain, it's too late — killing Glowstone in response doesn't stop the 5 damage; only the "kill this" is ignored, the damage still resolves (Rule 359.3.e.6). Only damage-prevention-type effects save their units.

question: when does glowstone damage deal, at the end of enemy's turn? or before scoring, and if they send it back, can i re-empower it and send it back again
answer:
Yes — the damage hits at the end of the enemy's turn, during their Ending Step (Rule 317.1.a), not before scoring. Glowstone's trigger is "At the end of your turn," so whoever controls it when their Ending Step arrives eats the 5 to all their units. Hold scoring already happened at the start of that same turn (Beginning Phase), so the damage always lands after that player's scoring for the turn.

After the trigger resolves, the Expiration Step cleanup kills units with lethal damage (Might 5 or less) and then heals everything else — the damage is gone by the next turn, but anything that died stays dead.

And yes, you can ping-pong it. When the enemy activates the send ability, they pay "Disempower this, [T]" as the cost, so it arrives at your Base exhausted and unempowered — you can't re-send it that same turn. But once your Awaken step readies it, you pay [A][A] to re-empower it (it's "not Empowered," so the ability is legal) and fire it back during your Main Phase. No per-turn or per-game limit; each cycle just costs the sender [A][A] + exhaust, and if a player does nothing it self-destructs and deals 5 at their own Ending Step.

question:
I saw lots of people saying that a hidden Zhonya’s Hourglass at a BF can only be played to the base because gears are not allowed to be played to the BF. If that’s the case, what is point of having the following rules?

811.1.d.1 A hidden permanent must be played to that battlefield.

811.1.d.1.a. This includes hidden gear, and overrides the normal restriction that gear have in only being allowed to be played to base.
answer:
Those people are wrong under the current rules — rule 811.1.d.1.a exists precisely to answer your question. A hidden gear is played to the battlefield where it was hidden, explicitly overriding the normal "gear only plays to base" restriction (Rules 148.1.a.1, 149.2). The "plays to base instead" claims come from older rules versions and older FAQ answers (e.g. FAQ #1533); the current Core Rules (2026-07-16) supersede them.

The catch is what happens right after: an unattached non-unit gear can't remain at a battlefield, so it's recalled to your base during the next Cleanup (CR 459.1). So the full sequence is: play Zhonya's from hidden at that battlefield → it resolves immediately and its replacement effect becomes active → the next Cleanup recalls it to base, where it keeps working (since it doesn't target, its effect is global — no "same battlefield" restriction, per the Origins patch clarification).

So the rule isn't pointless: it guarantees the gear physically enters at that battlefield first, which is what lets it function during the current showdown before being recalled. The only accurate version of the "base" claim is that the gear ends up in base at cleanup — not that it's played there.

question:
811.1.d.1.a. This includes hidden gear, and overrides the normal restriction that gear have in only being allowed to be played to base.

This core rule specifically mentions that a gear must be played to the BF, ignoring its original restriction. But then when the gear is played, it will be sent back to the base during a cleanup anyway since another rule says that a gear not being equipped to a unit cannot exist in a BF. Then what’s the point of the whole special mention and seemingly superseding rule?
answer:
The gear is not recalled instantly — it stays at that battlefield until the next Cleanup (CR 459.1, 149.3). That window is exactly the point.

First, the special mention in 811.1.d.1.a exists to resolve a rules conflict, not to create a lasting state. Playing from Hidden requires the permanent to enter at the battlefield where it was hidden (811.1.d.1), but Gear intrinsically "can only be played to a player's Base" (149.2). Without the override, playing a hidden gear would simply be illegal — the Hidden rule and the Gear rule would both be mandatory and contradictory. The recall rule (149.3/457.1) is a delayed corrective action that happens at the next Cleanup; it doesn't negate the entry location.

Second, a Cleanup can't run while items are on the chain — it's queued as an Outstanding Task (Rules 319, 321). So a hidden gear played as a Reaction enters at that battlefield and stays live there for the entire chain (and beyond). That's when its job gets done:

Zhonya's Hourglass: play from facedown for [0] as a Reaction when a friendly unit there would die — it enters at the battlefield and its replacement effect kills itself to save the unit (FAQ #1663). It's consumed before any cleanup ever sees it.

Edge of Night: its play effect attaches it to "a unit you control (here)" — it enters at the battlefield and immediately attaches to a unit there. Once attached it's no longer "unattached," so the recall rules never apply and it stays on the unit indefinitely.

The one genuine wrinkle: the "corrective action" wording in 149.3 reads like an immediate recall, but that's a known rulebook contradiction — the intended timing is recall at the next Cleanup (FAQ #4849). So the gear isn't shuttled back the moment it hits the board; it serves its purpose at the battlefield first.

question: Does Decree of Focus mistargets if the red unit in combat exits it? I attack Star Spring with one unit (Red) my opponent casts Decree of Focus on his unit, then I react with Nidalee and Star Spring triggers, and I send my red unit to base. How does this chain resolves?

Top of chain: Star Spring's trigger (from Nidalee entering via Ambush). It resolves first — you move your red unit to base.

A Cleanup occurs after that move. Your red unit is no longer at the combat battlefield, so it loses its Attacker designation (FAQ 2164; the unit that left is no longer "in combat").

Decree of Focus resolves: Its targeting requirement is "a friendly unit that's in combat with an enemy Fury unit." If you bounce the unit she intended to copy, that unit is no longer at the battlefield, so the copy effect fails for it. Temporary: Yes — Deceiver's own reflexive trigger reads "It becomes a copy of another unit there. Give it [Temporary]." The Temporary is granted directly by the legend ability, not copied from the target, so the token has it no matter what it copies and will die at the next beginning phase (Rule 816). This is confirmed by the official Zilean/Deceiver clarification, which notes Deceiver "gives the tokens Temporary."

question: I control 8 runes and 4 units. Opponent controls 4 gears and 8 runes. After Divine Judgment reasolves, what will remain on the board?
answer:
It depends on the choices, but here's what's guaranteed: after Divine Judgment resolves you'll have at least 2 of your units and 2 runes, and your opponent will have at least 2 gears and 2 runes.

Resolution works in turn order — you choose first (2 units, 2 gear, 2 runes, 2 hand cards), then your opponent chooses the same categories (FAQ #994). Every card not chosen is recycled simultaneously.

Key wrinkle for your board: choices aren't restricted to your own cards (FAQ #5977). You have 0 gears, so you must pick 2 of your opponent's 4 gears to keep — those 2 survive no matter what. Your opponent has 0 units, so they must pick 2 of your 4 units to keep — those 2 survive no matter what. Each of you keeps 2 of your own runes (2 each remain).

What survives beyond that is up to the second chooser. If your opponent picks the same 2 units you kept, your other 2 units get recycled (you end with 2 units). If they keep 2 different gears than the ones you saved, all 4 of their gears survive. So the realistic end state: you: 2 units + 2 runes; opponent: 4 gears + 2 runes — with the caveat that cooperative/overlapping picks can leave more units or fewer gears.

question: if i use thrill of the hunt will that properly dodge bounce or kill effects
answer:
Yes — but only against single-target bounce or kill spells that target the unit.

Thrill of the Hunt banishes the unit (a non-board zone) and replays it as a brand-new game object. Since moving to a non-board zone severs the targeting relationship, a spell already on the chain that targeted the original unit — like a "return to hand" or "kill" spell — will mistarget and fizzle against it (Rule 359.3.e; FAQ #10035, #10869).

Two big exceptions: it does not protect against non-targeting effects. Mass bounce/kill ("return all units", "kill all units") or board-wide damage (e.g., Unchecked Power) will still hit the replayed unit (FAQ #10753). And if an effect makes you kill one of your units without targeting (e.g., Cull of the Weak), the replayed unit is still on board and still a legal choice — you can't skip it (FAQ #11595).

question: What if opponent accidentally reveal opponent top deck
answer:
It depends on who saw the card, but the fix is to shuffle the accidentally revealed card back into its deck.

The top card of a deck is secret information — no one is entitled to it (CR 128). If a player accidentally flips over the top of a deck, that's a Looking at Secret Information [Warning] (TR 702.10). The remedy: shuffle the now-known card back into the randomized portion of its deck to remove the information advantage. If that's not possible, the card is revealed to all players and play continues.

If the erroring player accidentally reveals their own top card, the opponent who merely saw it gets no penalty — players aren't penalized for errors their opponents make (TR 702.10.a). The warning applies to the player who caused the reveal.

answer:

What does go on the Chain is its "when you play me" trigger. question: What is the difference between "finalize" and "resolution"?
answer:
Finalizing is completing the steps of playing an item (choices, costs, legality) and turning it from Pending into a Finalized Chain Item; resolution is the later step where the item's actual game effects execute.

Finalize is Step 1 of FEPR (Rule 337): the controller makes choices, determines and pays costs, and checks legality, then the item stops being Pending (Rule 359.1). No game effects happen here, and finalizing doesn't pass priority (Rule 337.1.a).

Resolve is Step 4 (Rule 340): the newest Finalized Chain Item executes its rules text in its entirety (Rule 340.1). For Units and Gear, finalize and resolve happen back-to-back — they leave the Chain and enter the board immediately (Rules 337.2, 359.2). Spells instead linger on the Chain after finalizing so opponents get a Reaction window, and only resolve later (Rule 359.3.c–d).

The practical difference: finalize = "is this card valid, paid for, and locked in?", resolve = "what does it actually do?"

question: What is restoring game state and deck state
answer:
Restoring game state and deck state are judge remedies for fixing errors — not a single mechanic.

Restoring the game state means rewinding the game to the state before an error occurred. Each action since the error is reversed in reverse order (TR 701.5). A simple rewind (only the most recent action) can be done by any judge; anything bigger requires the head judge or designated appeals judges. Any card whose identity became known during the error (e.g. a wrongly drawn card) is replaced with a random card so no information advantage survives, and any known cards in a deck are shuffled back into the randomized portion.

Restoring the deck state means making a deck's contents legal again after a setup/presentation error (TR 703.4, Deck Presentation Error) — undoing sideboarding for game one, pulling a Champion that was shuffled into the deck back to the Champion Zone, or fixing an illegal deck size. The judge moves cards back to their correct zones (including swapping sideboard cards out of a hand for random main-deck cards) and shuffles the randomized portion. If the deck can't be restored, the penalty escalates toward a Game Loss. Decks must also be returned to their registered state before the first game of the next match (TR 403.8).

question: In high opl when judge can interrupt a game?
answer:
A judge can interrupt a match at high OPL only in three situations: they believe a rules or policy violation has occurred, a player requests assistance, or they observe Unsporting Conduct (Rule 701.1.d).

Otherwise, judges are told not to intervene — they should not stop errors from occurring, only deal with errors that have already happened (Rule 701.1.c). Players can also pause at any time to flag a floor judge (Rule 412.1), and deck checks at high OPL are an allowed interruption (Rule 411). One important limit: a judge who discovers a previous ruling was wrong should wait until the current match is over rather than interrupt the ongoing game (FAQ 5409).

question: Can judge interrupt a game if a mandatory trigger miss in high opl?
answer:
Yes — a judge may pause a match to address a missed mandatory trigger at high OPL. Nothing in the Tournament Rules restricts judges to acting only when called: the Head Judge is explicitly responsible for ensuring rules are followed and violations are dealt with (TR 204.4.a–b), and judges may act on what they observe, including spectator alerts (TR 204.8.c).

Interrupting doesn't change the remedy, though. If the trigger was missed in the current turn, the next opponent in turn order decides whether it resolves immediately or is missed entirely (TR 702.2.f.2); if it was missed in a previous turn, play just continues (TR 702.2.f.1). A forgotten trigger never goes on the Chain (TR 506.4). question: Can you give me a riftbound layer?
answer:
There are three layers, and they loop until every applicable effect has been applied once and nothing changes (CR 478).

Trait-Altering (CR 479.2) — changes to Name, Supertype, Type, Tags, Controller, Cost, Domain. Copy effects and "Might becomes X" settings happen here.

Ability-Altering (CR 479.3) — grants/removes keywords, passive abilities, or rules text (e.g. "Other friendly units have Vision"), plus attached-card effect text.

Arithmetic (CR 479.4) — numeric +/- to Might, Energy Cost, Power Cost. Increases apply first, then decreases; non-passive limitations are snapshot at application.

Because layers loop, an effect applied in layer 3 can enable a layer-1/2 effect that wasn't applicable before — e.g. Fiora, Victorious: her Might buff bumps her past Mighty in the Arithmetic layer, then the sequence re-runs and she gains Deflect, Ganking, and Shield (CR 478.3, example). Within a single layer, dependencies apply first, otherwise timestamp order (FAQ 5401).

question: Can you show me riftbound layering
answer:
Sure — Riftbound's layers (CR 475–482) are the ordered system that decides how game effects modify traits, keywords, and numbers. There are three, applied top to bottom:

Trait-Altering (477.1) — changes to name, supertype, type, tags, controller, cost, domain, and Might-setting effects like "Might becomes 4." Copy effects (e.g. becoming a copy of another card) also apply here.

Ability-Altering (477.2) — granting/removing keywords and passive abilities, appending or removing rules text (including text from attached Gear).

Arithmetic (477.3) — the +/− math on Might and costs. Increases apply before decreases, and non-passive limits are "snapshotted" at the moment they apply.

After one pass through all three, the layers loop: re-evaluate and apply any effect that newly became applicable (476). Each effect only applies once per evaluation, and once a full pass changes nothing, you're done. That's what makes things like Fiora, Victorious work — her buff raises Might in Arithmetic, the loop re-checks Layer 2, and now "While I'm Mighty" grants her Deflect, Ganking, and Shield (476.3).

When multiple effects hit the same object in the same layer: check dependency first (if one effect's application changes the other's outcome, apply the depended-on one first — 478–479), otherwise fall back to timestamp order, earliest first (480).

question: How does snapshot work in riftbound
answer:
Snapshotting is Riftbound's rule that a non-passive effect's numbers are locked in ("remembered") at the moment the effect applies — they don't re-evaluate later.

CR 479.4.b: when an arithmetic effect that isn't a passive ability has a limitation (like a min/max or a target's current Might), that limitation is snapshotted at the time of application and kept at that level for the whole duration. Example: "-4 Might to a min of 1" on a 2-Might unit becomes a permanent (for the duration) -1, not a fluctuating -4 that re-checks.

Two key corollaries:

Passive abilities do NOT snapshot — they re-evaluate continuously ("Units you control here have 5 Might" stays live).

Spells/abilities DO snapshot at resolution — effects only apply to what's present when the spell resolves, and numbers are fixed then; things entering play later during the duration are not affected (FAQ #7876). This also interacts with layers: increases apply before decreases (477.3.e), each with their own snapshotted limitations.

question: Layering in riftbound explanation
answer:
Layers (CR 475–482) are the ordered system that decides how effects modify a card's traits, keywords, and numbers — and they loop until nothing changes.

There are three layers, applied top to bottom:

Trait-Altering (477.1) — name, supertype, type, tags, controller, cost, domain, copy effects, and Might setting ("Might becomes 4").

Ability-Altering (477.2) — granting/removing keywords and passive abilities, appending/removing rules text (including attached Gear text).

Arithmetic (477.3) — the +/− math on Might, Energy Cost, and Power Cost. Increases apply before decreases, and non-passive limitations are "snapshotted" when they apply.

The twist: after one pass, the sequence re-runs (CR 478). An effect applied in the Arithmetic layer can enable a layer-2 effect that wasn't applicable before. question: Definition of each layering in riftbound in simple definiton
answer:
Layers are the ordered system that decides how effects modify a card's traits, abilities, and numbers (CR 476–482). They apply top to bottom, then loop until nothing changes.

Trait-Altering — changes what a card is: Name, Supertype, Type, Tags, Controller, Cost, Domain, copy effects, and "Might becomes X" settings.

Ability-Altering — changes what a card does: granting/removing keywords, passive abilities, or rules text (including attached Gear text).

Arithmetic — the plain +/− math: Might, Energy Cost, Power Cost. Increases apply before decreases.

Because layers loop, a Layer 3 buff can enable a Layer 2 keyword — e.g., Fiora, Victorious gains her keywords only after her Might buff pushes her past "Mighty" (CR 478.4). Within one layer, dependent effects resolve dependencies first; otherwise timestamp order (CR 480–482).

question: Does layer always appear in every chain
answer:
No — layers and the Chain are separate game systems, and one does not imply the other.

Layers (CR 475–482) are the evaluation framework for how Game Effects alter traits, abilities, and numbers on objects. They run as part of continuous characteristic evaluation — whenever an effect needs to be applied, a chain or not. The Chain (CR 327–331) is a temporary zone that only exists while a card is being played or an ability activated.

So a Chain can form and resolve with zero layer activity (e.g., drawing a card, dealing damage), and layers get applied constantly outside any Chain (passive auras, buff counters, Combat Cleanup). The two only interact in that a resolved effect may cause a layer evaluation — but layers are not a Chain item, step, or event.

question: Can you empower renekton any number of time in risen altar
answer:
No — you can't. Risen Altar only discounts actual Empower keyword costs, and Renekton, Brute doesn't have one — and nothing on either card grants the special permission to become Empowered more than once.

Risen Altar reads "[Empower] costs of your units here cost [1] or [A] less." This only reduces costs printed with the Empower keyword (e.g., "Empower [2]"). Renekton, Brute's activated ability is "[1]: Give me +1 Might this turn" — that's a pump ability, not an Empower ability (his Keywords line shows Empowered/Deflect/Ganking only).

Even for units that do have Empower, Rule 827.1.c.1 makes it "Play only if not Empowered." Once a unit gains the Empowered status, the ability can't activate again — unless a card text explicitly grants permission to be Empowered multiple times (CR 442.1.c.1). Risen Altar grants no such permission; it's purely a cost modifier.

Renekton's "When my Might becomes 10 or more, empower me" fires once when he crosses that threshold for the first time (and only if he wasn't already Empowered — "empower me. I become Empowered if I'm not already"). If he's already at 10+, the "become" event never re-occurs (FAQ #11768).

If you disempower Renekton (e.g., with Profiteer), then yes, you could empower him again later — but that's a separate removal/restoration of the status, not "any number of times" from Risen Altar.

question: What happen if I cast a targeting spell without paying the deflect cost? Will the spell still go onto the chain?
answer:
No — without paying Deflect, the play is illegal and the spell never becomes a final chain item. Deflect is a mandatory additional cost paid while you finalize the play (choosing targets and paying costs), so a spell that targets a Deflect permanent can't be legally placed on the Chain unless that cost is paid (Rule 809.1.c–d, FAQ #7667).

If you can't pay, the play is undone: the card returns to your hand and it doesn't count as "playing a spell" for triggers. If you merely forgot to pay but a legal alternative target exists, a judge may rewind only the targeting step so you choose a legal target instead of a full undo. Either way, the spell does not sit on the Chain unpaid — Deflect costs aren't applied retroactively, so once it's a finalized chain item it's too late.

Deflect isn't optional: it reads as "spells and abilities an opponent controls that choose me cost [X] more Power to play as an additional cost for each time they choose me" (Rule 809.1.c–d). You have to use Akali's ability during the Non-Combat Showdown, while you have Focus (Rule 347.1). question: Can repeat cost be reduced with applied researcher
answer:
Yes — while Applied Researchers is Empowered, its discount reduces a Repeat cost, but only the one you actually choose to pay.

Repeat is an optional additional cost added to the base cost when you declare it (Rule 820.1), and discounts are applied to that combined total once (Rule 356.4.f — same treatment as Eager Apprentice, FAQ #629). So the Empowered discount — spells cost 1 Energy less (minimum 1) and 1 any-domain Power less — shaves the Repeat cost together with the base cost, not twice. If you don't declare Repeat, there's nothing extra to discount; and if the spell's Energy cost is already at the 1 floor, the Energy part of the discount won't help, though a Power-denominated Repeat (e.g. Repeat [A] or [C]) would still get the [A] Power discount.

question: Applied researcher with deflect and repeat costs
answer:

Since discounts can reduce additional costs to 0 (Rule 356.4.f), the "[1][A] less" from Applied Researchers covers a Deflect 1 surcharge — you pay your normal cost, not the extra Power, when your spell chooses a Deflect unit.

Two limits: it only applies to spells you play (not your activated abilities, and not reflexive triggers your spells create), and it only works while Applied Researchers is Empowered (pay [3] first). It also doesn't bypass Deflect's targeting rule — the cost is still added and then discounted, and if Deflect is higher than 1 you still pay the remainder.

Because that unit is still present, the attacker keeps their presence at the location and keeps the Attacker designation — control isn't lost while chain items are pending, and the Ambush unit alone is enough to hold the attack (mirror of FAQ #10057).

Two important catches:

Timing: you can't react to the Ambush play itself — units finalize and enter immediately with no window (FAQ #9978). You're actually reacting to the window created by the Ambush unit's enter/attack triggers (or another chain item), not to the play.

Cost: Star-Crossed requires both a friendly and an enemy unit, so you must also return one of your own units. If that was your only unit at that battlefield, you're left with zero units while the attacker's Ambush unit remains — when the combat resolves, the attacker wins and establishes control, Conquering the battlefield (CR 468).

So the only way this plays out well for you as the defender is if you still have another unit (or a play that replaces the bounced one) to keep defenders present.

question: Akali silent is at a battlefield. Enemy Zenith Blade, moving a unit to the battlefield. Will it also stun Akali now she is in combat when the enemy unit moves?
answer:
No — Zenith Blade can't stun Akali here, and the enemy can't even legally choose her as its target.

Akali's passive makes her unchoosable by enemy spells and abilities unless she is in combat, and she isn't in combat at the moment Zenith Blade is played and its target is chosen — sitting alone at a battlefield (even in a Non-Combat Showdown) gives her no Attacker/Defender designation (Rules 758, 355.9.b; her card text). A future state your own spell creates can't retroactively validate the choice (Rule 355.9, cf. FAQ #1492).

It also wouldn't help during resolution: Zenith Blade's instructions run in order — stun first, then the move — and combat designations only get assigned during a Cleanup with an empty chain, well after the spell has fully resolved (CR 323.2, 461–462). So Akali is still not "in combat" at the instant the stun instruction would apply.

If she were already a participant in an ongoing Combat Showdown (attacker or defender designation) when Zenith Blade is played, she'd be a perfectly legal stun target — but the move alone can't put her in combat in time.

question: What happens if i cast sanction to empower Kharox and then cast another sanction to disempower it. Do the end of turn effect of each sanction still trigger?
answer:
Yes — both end-of-turn effects still trigger, because each Sanction created its own Delayed Ability that fires on its own schedule regardless of what happened in between (CR 393).

Casting the second Sanction (mode 2, "Disempower... Empower it at end of turn") does not cancel the first Sanction's pending "Disempower it at end of turn." At the Ending Step both delayed triggers go on the chain. Since you control both, you choose their order (Rule 383.3.d).

Sanction #1's delayed disempower: if Kharox is already disempowered when it resolves, it does nothing (CR 443.1.a.1).

Sanction #2's delayed empower: it will still Empower Kharox at end of turn — and since Kharox is no longer Empowered at that point, this is a new Empower event that retriggers his "When I become Empowered" (Burn 3, then optionally play a unit from their trash).

Ordering matters only for the final state: if Sanction #2's empower resolves last, Kharox ends the turn Empowered; if Sanction #1's disempower resolves last, it removes the status. Note Empowered isn't a "this turn" effect, so whichever empowerment survives the Ending Step carries into the next turn.

One catch: if Tideturner is played to your Base (not from Hidden), a unit already at Base is at the same location and cannot be chosen — the target must be at "another location" (FAQ 7937).

question: Will Jayce brilliant inventor trigger on itself and the first non-toke gear played each turn?
answer:
Yes — those are two separate trigger conditions on the same ability, and both can fire in one turn.

Playing Jayce fulfills the "when you play me" clause, and since Jayce is a Unit, not a Gear (Rule 148), that play does not count as — or use up — the "first non-token gear" clause. If you then play your first non-token gear that turn while Jayce is still in play, that clause triggers separately.

So in a clean sequence — play Jayce, then later play your first non-token gear — you may ready once per trigger, up to two different exhausted things (never Jayce himself). Each individual trigger still only readies one thing. Note the gear clause can only fire if the first non-token gear is played after Jayce is on the board; a gear played before he arrives doesn't set it off.

question: Can Zed’s Shadow Clones conquer an open battlefield with zero might? Can it also hold a battlefield alone with zero might?
answer:
Yes to both — a unit's Might has nothing to do with Control, Conquering, or Holding.

A 0-Might Shadow Clone is still a unit (Rule 187.11), and control is established purely by having your units present at a battlefield at the end of a Showdown. If a clone is the only unit at an open battlefield when the Non-Combat Showdown closes, you establish Control and Conquer it for 1 point if you haven't already scored that battlefield this turn (CR 348.2.a, 471.1). Similarly, it can Hold: a clone sitting there alone during your Beginning Phase keeps you in Control and nets the Hold point (CR 190.4.a, 471.2).

The real vulnerability is combat, not Might: in a Combat Showdown the clone adds 0 damage to your pool and dies to any non-zero damage assigned to it (CR 467.2.c.2). And the normal once-per-battlefield-per-turn scoring limit still applies.

So a Reflection copy of her (e.g., from Deceiver) has her passive plus the granted [Temporary], and at the start of your Beginning Phase the kill trigger simply never fires — Rule 816.

question: If Trusty Ramhound is defending at a battlefield with an ally, the ally is assigned lethal damage from the combat resolution, and the Trusty Ramhound is assigned two remaining damage, will Trusty Ramhound live?
answer:
Yes — Trusty Ramhound survives.

Here's why: Trusty Ramhound is Might 3 while its ally is present (base 2 + the +1 Might from its ability). At the combat cleanup's kill check, the game evaluates lethal damage for all units at one point in time while the ally is still alive — so Ramhound has only 2 damage marked against Might 3, which is not lethal. The ally is killed in that same simultaneous event, and then the Combat Special Cleanup's "Heal all Units" step (CR 468.1.a.1) removes Ramhound's 2 damage before any later check can kill it. Even though Ramhound's Might drops to 2 when the ally dies, its damage is already healed.

This matches the established Lee Sin aura rulings (FAQ #5961, #7339) and FAQ #2301: "A unit that would drop to lethal damage after another unit dies will survive if it heals during the cleanup." Note that this only works because healing happens during the same combat cleanup — outside combat (e.g., a kill spell removing the ally), Ramhound would take lethal in the subsequent cleanup.

question: If Trusty Ramhound is defending at a battlefield with an ally, the ally is assigned lethal damage from the combat resolution, and the Trusty Ramhound is assigned two remaining damage, will Trusty Ramhound live?
answer:
Yes — Trusty Ramhound lives.

Combat damage is all dealt at once, and the Combat Cleanup kills lethal-damage units before it heals — but the lethal check happens while the ally is still on the board. Ramhound is at 3 Might (2 base + 1 from the ally), so 2 damage isn't lethal; only the ally dies in the kill step, then Combat Cleanup's "heal all units" removes Ramhound's 2 damage before anything can re-check it (CR 323.4, 468.1.a.1; FAQ #7339/#5961).

A cleaner way to see it: a cleanup can't be interrupted mid-way — nothing between the kill step and the heal step re-evaluates Ramhound's Might. Note the caveat: this survival is specific to combat. If the ally died to spell damage instead, the subsequent non-combat cleanup would have no healing step, and Ramhound would then be killed once its Might dropped to 2 with 2 damage marked (FAQ #7339).

question: In 4 players FFA How meny players can be at the same battlefield while showdown? And how to deal with cards that can create this situation like moonfall and Irresistible Faefolk
answer:
Max is 2 players — combat (and any showdown) only ever involves exactly two players' units in FFA4 (CR 464).

A third player can never have units at the battlefield where a showdown/combat is occurring. That battlefield is an Invalid Destination for their units' moves (CR 449.2.a, 464.1), they can't play units into it (CR 464.2 — they'd go to Base instead), and no unit may move to a battlefield already holding two other players' units "by any means" (CR 451.2). So while other players can cast spells during your showdown (turn order from the attacker), their units cannot be there.

Moonfall and Irresistible Faefolk cannot force a third player into an existing fight. The enemy unit they move is subject to the same destination rules: if it's controlled by a player not involved in the combat who has no units there, the destination is invalid, and the choice itself is "invalid and ineligible to be completed" (CR 464.3). Since both effects are optional ("you may"), you simply move nothing. You can only use them to (a) pull a unit from an enemy who already has units at that battlefield (that unit just becomes the defender), or (b) start a fresh 2-player fight at a battlefield where only you have units — e.g., during someone else's showdown, target a different battlefield you hold; that new fight stages and waits for the current one to finish (FAQ #5108). Moonfall's -2 penalty still hits enemy units there even if you move no one.

question: If I play a Temporal Breach on a unit that my opponent played from my discard with Kharox and is now on a battlefield, will my unit be played on that battlefield?

That location is a battlefield, and you're allowed to play a unit there even though your opponent controls it — doing so applies Contested status (Rules 190.3.a, 355.2). Ownership never changed when Kharox played your unit from your trash; Kharox's controller only gained control of it on the board.

If your opponent still has units at that battlefield, a Combat Showdown stages against them once play resumes. If they've moved their other units away, it's just a Non-Combat Showdown. The one case where this breaks is if the unit was in your opponent's Base — you can't legally play a unit to an opponent's base, so that instruction is negated and the unit stays banished (FAQ 12422; Rules 359.3.e.6, 355.2.a).

question: Can a 0 might reflection unit (copied something that got star crossed or gust or killed) can conqueer or hold ?
answer:
Yes. A 0 Might Reflection is still a unit, and Might has nothing to do with Control, Conquering, or Holding — same as Zed's 0 Might Shadow Clones (FAQ #12473). It can walk onto an empty battlefield you don't control, win the Non-Combat Showdown by being the only unit present, establish Control, and Conquer for a point (CR 348.2.a, 471.1).

Two important caveats:

If the Reflection already finished copying before the original got Star-Crossed/Gusted/killed, it isn't 0 Might at all — a finished copy effect persists, so it keeps the copied unit's Might and text even after the original leaves. The "0 Might Reflection" only exists when the copy was stopped in response (copy target gone before the effect resolved, FAQ #10681).

A Reflection from Mirror Image/Deceiver always ends up with Temporary — the grant isn't tied to the copy succeeding (FAQ #11492). Temporary kills it at the start of its controller's Beginning Phase, before scoring (Rule 816.1.b), so it will die before the Hold scoring step. If it's alone on a battlefield when that happens, you lose Control in the cleanup and get no Hold point — the Reflection can conquer during the window it lives, but it can't be the unit that Holds. (Without Temporary, a 0 Might Reflection would hold fine.)

Combat is where 0 Might hurts: if the battlefield it moves to has enemy units, it adds 0 damage and dies to anything assigned to it — conquering only works against empty/uncontested battlefields.

question: does mel newly awakened when empowered give additional - might when applying switcheroo?
answer:
Yes — an Empowered Mel does add the extra -1 [M], applied to the unit on the losing side of the swap.

Swap isn't a single value-setting action: CR 434.1.a/b says a swap creates two effects — an Increase for the difference on the lower-Might unit and a Decrease of that same amount on the higher-Might unit. That Decrease is a "give -[M]" event to a unit your spell chose (Switcheroo targets both units), so Mel's replacement effect (Rule 370.1) replaces it with a Decrease of one more.

Example: unit A at 5 [M], unit B at 2 [M] at the same battlefield → Switcheroo gives A -3 (Mel makes it -4, so A ends at 1 [M]) and B +3 (B ends at 5 [M]). The swap is therefore no longer a perfect reversal. Only the -[M] side is affected — Mel never touches the Increase.

Edge case: if both units have the same Might, CR 434.1.c says the swap does nothing, so no -[M] event occurs and Mel adds nothing (same logic as the official Stupefy-on-a-1-[M]-unit ruling, FAQ #11759). This all assumes Mel is Empowered and you control the Switcheroo.

question: Does shady spectacles also copy a cards tags? So if I have breakneck mech and copy a plaza guardian, will the plaza guardian get the bonuses from breakneck mech?

But the follow-up depends on which unit is wearing the Spectacles. If Breakneck Mech is the equipped unit and it copies Plaza Guardian, it stops being Breakneck Mech entirely — it keeps Mech as a tag (Plaza Guardian is a Mech), but it loses Breakneck Mech's own rules text, so "Your Mechs have [Deflect] and [Ganking]" is gone and nothing else gets that bonus.

Deflect is a stacking keyword, so Breakneck Mech + a copy of Breakneck Mech will give all your Mechs Deflect 2. Ganking does not stack stack though.

question: Can you chain reactions?
answer:
Yes — you can. Once a chain exists the turn is in a Closed State, and only Reaction-speed cards and abilities can be added to it, so any number of Reactions can stack on top of each other (Rule 309.1.a, 813).

They resolve last-in-first-out, and there's a fresh priority window after each item resolves — both players get a chance to add another Reaction before the next item resolves. So you can keep the chain going at every step, not just at the initial play.

One limit: a Reaction is still a Reaction. You can't slip an Action, a unit, or a non-Reaction activated ability onto an existing chain — wait for it to clear.

question: Define hold
answer:
Hold is the scoring method where a player keeps control: you Hold when you maintain Control of a battlefield you have not yet scored this turn, during your Beginning Phase (CR 471.2). It's the passive counterpart to Conquer — Conquer is gaining Control of a battlefield you didn't control; Hold is still controlling one when your turn begins.

When you Hold, you gain up to 1 point (subject to the Final Point restrictions that apply only to Conquer, CR 473.1.a.1), and any "when I hold / when you hold" abilities trigger at the battlefield that was Held (CR 473.2.b) — these are Hold Effects and go on the Chain as Pending Items. Hold happens as part of the Beginning phase of your turn.

One limit matters in practice: you can only score each battlefield once per turn, so a battlefield you already Conquered this turn can't also be Held for a second point (CR 472).

question: What happens if switcheroo is played on forbidding waste where one player the attacker has a 5 might unit and the other has a 1 might unit defending
answer:
They swap — the attacker's unit becomes 1 Might and the defending unit becomes 5 Might, and Forbidding Waste's -2 keeps applying to the defender on top of that.

Switcheroo swaps the units' current Might (CR 434.1.b: take the difference, increase the lower value and decrease the higher), so the battlefield's -2 is already baked into the defender's 1 when the swap is calculated. The -2 then continues to apply afterward, because Forbidding Waste is a passive "while defending alone" effect that re-evaluates continuously — the defender is still defending alone, so nothing falls off (FAQ #10921).

Practical consequence: since damage uses current Might at the Combat Damage Step (CR 467.2), the 1-Might attacker assigns only 1 damage to the 5-Might defender, while the defender assigns 5 to the attacker's unit — almost certainly killing it. Note the swap only lasts this turn.

question: What's the process of playing a gear, how does equip work, when can I play a gear and equip it, where can the unit be when I equip a gear?
answer:
Short version: Play the gear to your Base (it enters ready), then use its Equip ability — an activated ability usable in your Main Phase during an Open State — to attach it to any unit you control, wherever that unit is.

Playing a gear. Pay its cost; it goes on the Chain, finalizes, and resolves immediately — units and gear skip Execute/Pass, so opponents get no reaction window to the play itself (FAQ #8333). By default gear enters your Base, ready (Rules 149.1–149.2), and can be played on your turn in an Open State.

How Equip works. Equip is an Activated Ability: [Cost]: Attach this gear to a unit you control (Rule 818.1.c.2). It behaves like a spell without a card — it goes on the Chain, so the state closes and opponents can respond with Reactions to it (FAQ #9560). Standard timing is your Main Phase, Open State, and not during a Showdown (Rules 151.2, 381) — so it's neither an Action nor a Reaction (FAQ #1120). Once the gear is attached its rules text goes inactive, so you can't use that Equip ability to move it off (Rules 718.2, FAQ #2139); you can still pile multiple gears on one unit (FAQ #6479).

Timing after playing. Yes — you can play a gear and immediately Equip it in the same Main Phase, as long as you have the resources for the Equip cost and the state is Open with no Showdown running. Quick-Draw is the exception: it grants Reaction inherently and auto-attaches on play (Rule 819.1.d), letting you play and attach at Reaction timing.

Where the unit can be. Anywhere you control it — your Base or a Battlefield you control; Equip has no location restriction on the target unit. If you equip a unit at a battlefield, the gear becomes located there through the Attach action (Rule 152.2); if that unit later dies, the gear stays at that battlefield and gets Recalled to your Base at the next Cleanup (CR 459, 149.3).

question: When Switcheroo swaps current Might values between two units, does the Forbidding Waste penalty get counted once in the swap calculation, or does it apply separately on top of the swapped values?
answer:
Counted once — the −2 is part of the unit's current Might when Switcheroo resolves, and it then keeps applying as an ongoing static effect rather than being added a second time.

Switcheroo determines the difference between the two units' current Might (CR 434.1.b), so Forbidding Waste's −2 is already baked into that number and the swap modifier is sized to hit the correct totals. Unlike a spell effect, Forbidding Waste is a passive "while" ability, so it doesn't snapshot — it re-evaluates continuously (CR 479.4.b, FAQ #10921).

Practical result: after the swap the unit at Forbidding Waste still has the −2 applied on top of the fixed swap modifier. Example — lone defender base 4 (currently 2 with the penalty) swaps with a 6 Might unit: the defender ends at 4 − 2 + 4 = 6 and the other unit at 2. question: My opponent casts Promising Future, banishing Elder Dragon. I banish Fizz. At which point do I choose the spell Fizz replays? When this happens, can I target his Elder with a Star-Crossed replayed from Fizz?
answer:
You pick the trash spell when Fizz's "when you play me" ability is finalized onto the chain — not when Fizz hits the board — and by that point Elder Dragon is already in play, so Star-Crossed can legally choose it.

Here's the flow. And remember, finalize up the chain, resolve down the chain.
Your Fizz enters pending first.
Opponent's Dragon enters pending right after.
Fizz finalizes and resolves, Fizz' 'When you play me' goes as a pending item on the chain.
Dragon finalizes and resolves, Dragon's 'When you play me' goes as a pending item on the chain.
Fizz' ability finalizes -> choice of spell is made here.
Dragon's ability finalizes -> targets are chosen.
Dragon's ability resolves.
Fizz's ability resolves -> the chosen spell becomes a pending chain item.
Finalize the chosen spell -> pick it's targets.
Resolve the spell.

It might very well be that Fizz is already dead by the time your Star-Crossed resolves. But during finalization of Star-Crossed you can pick targets. You need 1 friendly and 1 enemy unit for legal target allocation.

question: If a flow card is in trash, and you conquer with Kennen, can I play using kennen’s flow cost instead?
answer:
Yes — you choose. Both the printed Flow cost and Kennen's granted Flow cost become instances of Flow on the same spell, and the controller picks which one to apply when playing it (Rule 829.1.c.3).

Worth knowing: Kennen's granted cost is "equal to its cost," which is checked against the spell's printed cost (CR 206) — so it's usually the base cost, and for most Flow spells (e.g. Shadow Dash at [5][A][A]) Kennen's grant is the cheaper option. You're never forced to use it; if the printed Flow cost is lower, take that one.

Two timing notes: the grant only lasts that turn, and Kennen's "When I conquer" trigger resolves as the showdown closes/control is established, so there's no showdown window left at that instant (FAQ #12519) — you need a later legal window that same turn (a Showdown for an Action spell, or any priority if the spell has Reaction if these happen on your opponents turn or during your turn when the turn is in the Neutral Open state, which is when no Chain exists and there is no Showdown active). Either way, playing it from trash banishes it after it resolves.

The "when you play me" instance is placed when Kennen enters (Rule 383.4.a.2); because Ava plays him "here" into the battlefield where her combat is ongoing, he then gains the Attacker designation during the next Cleanup along with his controller (Rule 323.2.a), which places the attack-trigger instance (Rule 383.4.e.2). Arriving late to a combat still counts — that's the same principle as FAQ #4095/#716.

Each instance is a separate "you may pay [2] to stun a unit," so you decide independently for each: pay for one, both, or neither, and you choose the order if they're placed simultaneously (Rule 383.3.d). Note Ava plays him from hand, not from Hidden, so neither stun is restricted to targeting units at his battlefield. If he's played somewhere he never becomes an attacker (e.g.: base, if Ava's moved to base before her trigger resolves), you get only the single play trigger.

Timing: Viktor's trigger is placed on the chain as a pending item while Jayce's play effect is resolving, so it finalizes and resolves after Jayce's ability finishes — you play the Recruit token into your base, and you can still play the gear from hand any time later that turn (per the Jayce clarification).

No. Sivir, Battle Mistress (Battle Mistress) has exactly two triggers: "When you recycle a rune, you may exhaust me to play a Gold gear token exhausted" and "When one or more enemy units die, ready me." Killing a Gold gear token satisfies neither.

A Gold token is a gear, not a unit (Rule 187.5), so its death never counts as "an enemy unit dies." And killing a gear is not recycling a rune — recycling is a specific action that moves a rune back into your rune deck, not a Kill (CR 429). Note also that when you kill the Gold via its own ability ("Kill this, [E]: [Add] [A]"), the kill is a cost, not a recycle, so nothing about that sequence touches Sivir.

So the only ways to fire Sivir are a genuine rune recycle (for the Gold token trigger) or an enemy unit actually dying (for the ready trigger).

answer:
Yes, but not many — and there's no "Law" domain in Riftbound (the domains are Order, Chaos, Calm, Body, Mind, Fury; "Keeper of Law" is simply an Order card).

For playing out of the trash, Order has Spectral Matron, Glasc Mixologist (on Deathknell), and the spell Undying Loyalty — each plays a unit from your trash ignoring its cost. question: I was using OGS-019 Master Yi, and I had a Pouty Poro on a battlefield. Enemy had a Ravenbloom Student and an Eager Apprentice in the base. It was the enemy’s turn. He moved the Apprentice to my battlefield and started a combat showdown. He started a chain with Smoke Screen targeting my Poro. I passed and let it resolve. Then I started a chain with Discipline and it resolved. He passed focus and I casted Rune Prison on his Apprentice, he reacted with a Stupefy on my Poro. And the showdown ended with no unit died, and the Apprentice was sent back to the base. He then attacked with the Ravenbloom student. What should be the might of my Poro at this point?
answer:
Your Poro is 2 Might when it defends against the Ravenbloom Student.

The key is what Smoke Screen saw when it resolved. By then the Apprentice had already moved in and the combat showdown had started, so your Poro was the lone defender and Wuju Bladesman's "defending alone" passive was live — its Might was 2 + 2 = 4. question: all types of chain?
answer:
There's only one Chain — Riftbound doesn't have "types" of chains. Rule 330.1: only one Chain can exist at a time, and any new card or ability played while it exists gets added to that same chain (330.2).

What does have categories is the items on it. Every chain item is either Pending or Finalized: it's added as a Pending Item and becomes Finalized after the Check Legality step of playing it (Rule 329). Items that can sit on the chain are cards (units, gear, spells), tokens, and abilities — activated, triggered, and reflexive (CR 328.1, 389).

One practical split worth knowing: permanents (units and non-unit gear) leave the chain when finalized and hit the board immediately (Rule 359.2), while spells linger on the chain as Finalized items until they resolve (359.3). Everything resolves last-in-first-out (Rule 340.1).

question: What opens a chain outside and inside of showdowns?
answer:
One thing opens a chain everywhere: an item becoming Pending. Three sources — playing a card, activating an ability, or a triggered ability becoming Pending (CR 328, 402.1). When it isn't your turn you would need a triggered ability or a showdown to be able to start a chain; only one chain exists at a time, so "starting a chain" only applies when no chain exists yet (Rule 330).

Outside a showdown (Neutral Open): the default opener is the turn player in their Main Phase, playing a card or activating an ability. Note the state immediately becomes Closed once that happens, so follow-ups need Reaction. Triggered abilities can add items in any state, on anyone's turn.

Inside a showdown: the player with Focus may start a chain with a card or activated ability that is legally timed — during Showdown Open that means Action or Reaction by default; nothing else is playable (Rule 347.1). Each spell played this way creates a chain as normal (Rule 342.1), and once a chain exists only Reactions can be added. Triggered abilities still land on the chain (e.g. attacker/defender triggers form the Combat Chain when combat opens).

One subtlety: a Reaction can be the first item of a chain, since Reaction grants all Action permissions plus Closed-State play.

question: what are the steps of a chain in and outside of a showdown
answer:
Same four steps either way — the FEPR loop (Finalize → Execute → Pass → Resolve, Rules 337–340). Only the permissions and what happens when the chain empties differ.

Finalize: each controller completes the play steps for their Pending items in the order they were added; units, gear, and Add-resource abilities resolve immediately on finalizing (337.2). Execute: the player with Priority (in a showdown, the player with Focus) plays a legally timed card/ability or passes — in a Closed State outside a showdown that means Reaction only, while in a Showdown Closed state an Action card that opened the chain is also fine (338.1.a.2, 358.4). Pass: if everyone passes in sequence without adding anything, go to Resolve; otherwise priority moves to the next player in turn order. Resolve: the newest item resolves fully (LIFO), then back to Finalize if the chain isn't empty, or the turn returns to an Open State if it is.

The real divergence is after that last resolution: during a showdown, Focus passes to the next player in turn order (340.2.a) — except when the chain was opened by a triggered ability or an Add ability, in which case the player whose Focus it was, will keep Focus (346.1). Outside a showdown there's no Focus at all; the turn simply returns to Neutral Open and, after any cleanup, the Turn Player gets priority back in their Main Phase.

question: can a token exist without its owner card. for example zed making a shadow token
answer:
Yes — tokens don't need any owner card to exist. Tokens are their own category of Game Object, not cards (Rule 185), so a Shadow Clone created by Zed, Without a Sound exists on the board purely as a token.

Its "owner" is just defined as whoever controlled the effect that created it (Rule 183), which is Zed's controller — no physical card is required or tracked. The token persists on its own even if Zed later leaves play; the only thing that makes it vanish is being put into a non-board zone other than the Chain (Rule 186.1), e.g. if it's killed into the trash. So a token can't "exist" in your hand, deck, or trash, but on the board it's a fully independent object.

question: Complete list of everything that can be reacted to
answer:
Short answer: you can react to anything that stays on the Chain as a finalized item. Reaction isn't about "responding" to arbitrary events — it's a permission to play/activate during a Closed State, so a window only exists if something is sitting on the chain.

Reactable:

Spells — they linger on the chain after finalizing (Rule 359.3), so opponents get priority before resolution.

Triggered abilities of any sort — "When you play me," "When I attack/defend," "When I move," Deathknell, reflexive triggers, etc. (Rule 383).

Activated abilities, including Equip and any gear/unit/legend ability with [Reaction][>] or [Action][>] (Rule 818.1). Reactions can also stack on other Reactions.

Any of the above during a Combat Showdown, as well as combat triggers like "When I attack."

Not reactable:

Playing a unit or gear — permanents leave the chain the moment they finalize, so no window exists (Rule 359.2). You can react to any "When you play me" trigger the permanent creates.

Hiding a card — discretionary, no chain.

Discretionary actions that don't use the chain: Standard Move, Recalls, scoring/Conquer/Hold, combat damage, cleanup steps (FAQ #5996, #2835).

Add abilities and tapping runes for mana — these finalize and resolve immediately, even mid-resolution, so nothing lingers to respond to (CR 430.2, FAQ #3799).

One practical note: Reaction isn't strictly "responding." On your own turn you can play a Reaction with an empty chain just like an Action spell; it's only priority that limits you on an opponent's turn (FAQ #11498).

question: Can battlefield triggers be reacted to?
answer:
Yes — battlefield triggered abilities go on the Chain like any other triggered ability, and once an item is on the Chain the state is Closed, so players may respond with Reactions (Rule 383.3, 813.1.c).

The catch is that there must actually be a trigger to respond to. Battlefield abilities only trigger when their condition is genuinely met — e.g. a Hold ability only fires if a unit was present at that battlefield when its controller scored the point, so with no units there and no Hold, nothing goes on the Chain and there's no window (FAQ #10348). Also remember triggered-ability targets are locked at finalization, so you can react, but you can't react to a trigger and then have a newly revealed unit become its target.

question: Can I react to shens “when I hold with one other unit I score” or any passive type abilities
answer:
Yes for Shen's hold ability — no for genuine passive abilities.

Shen, Leader of the Kinkou Order reads "[Shield] When I hold, if there is exactly one other unit you control here, you score 1 point." The "when I hold" clause makes this a Hold Effect, i.e. a triggered ability, so it's put on the chain as a pending item and every player gets a Reaction window before it resolves (Rule 383.4.d). What you can't react to is the hold/score event that caused it.

One nuance: the "exactly one other unit you control here" clause sits immediately after the trigger condition, so it's part of the condition, not the effect (Rule 383.2.a.1) — it's checked when the trigger fires, and killing that other unit in response won't stop the point. Once the trigger is on the chain it resolves.

Passive abilities are different: they're statements of fact with no "when/at" condition (Shield is a passive, for example), they never use the chain, and there is no priority window in which to react to them — they just continuously apply.

question: Can a Champion Legend be played?
answer:
No — a Champion Legend is never "played." It's established at the start of the game: each player places their Champion Legend in the Legend Zone during setup, and it stays there for the duration of regular play (Rules 174.2.a–174.2.b, 111).

Everything it does, it does from that zone. Legends can have Passive, Triggered, and Activated abilities, can be targeted by spells and game effects, and can't be Killed or Moved (Rules 174.3–174.8). question: can you react to astral heron trigger, can you play a reaction speed card between 2 heron triggers on Bfs assuming they both flat the trigger already
answer:
It depends which "between" you mean — you cannot insert a Reaction between the two Herons triggering, but you can play one between their resolutions.

Both Herons trigger simultaneously when you play your first card, so they go on the chain together as pending items, with you choosing their order (Rule 383.3.d). Finalizing doesn't pass priority (Rule 337.1.a), so there's no window to act until all pending items are done — the opponent can't slip a Reaction in ahead of the second trigger being queued.

Once the first Heron trigger resolves, though, priority goes to the controller of the next item on the chain (Rule 340.4), so you get a genuine window before the second trigger resolves. The chain is non-empty there, so it's a Closed State: only Reaction cards/abilities are legal.

One real consequence: a card played in that window is "the next card you play this turn," so it would consume the first Heron's discount, leaving the second Heron's discount for the card after that — you'd have to actually want that. If your goal is stacking both discounts on one card, just pass and let both triggers resolve (FAQ #11679).

question: I go on an uncontested battlefield with vi peacekeeper, my opponent plays rengar trophy hunter on it using rengar's reaction speed ambush, can Vi stun the rengar? If yes, who stays at the battlefield?
answer:
Yes — Vi still stuns Rengar, and Rengar ends up staying at the battlefield while Vi is recalled to Base.

Moving Vi to an empty battlefield only starts a Non-Combat Showdown, so she doesn't have the Attacker designation yet. Once your opponent plays Rengar there, the showdown converts into a Combat Showdown, and the Attacker is the player whose unit applied Contested — you — so Vi gains the Attacker designation and her "When I attack" trigger fires, stunning Rengar (FAQ #12636). She does need to still be at the battlefield when the trigger resolves.

In the Combat Damage Step, stunned Rengar contributes no Might, so only Vi's 5 damage is assigned to a 6-Might Rengar — not lethal, and he heals in the Combat Cleanup anyway. Because a Defender is still present, the Attacker is recalled (CR 468.1.a.2): Vi returns to your Base (unharmed), and Rengar's controller remains the only player with units there, so they Establish Control and Conquer.

question: Can an empowered Ambessa, The Wolf be targeted by abilities that kill?
answer:
Yes. Empowered Ambessa, The Wolf can be targeted by kill abilities — her Empowered text only stops damage, not targeting or destruction.

While Empowered she reads "I have +3 [M] and can't be dealt damage unless I'm in combat." That is a damage-prevention effect only (and "can't" beats "deal" for damage effects, Rule 54). A kill instruction like "Kill a unit at a battlefield" doesn't deal damage, so nothing in her text interacts with it — she can be chosen and killed normally, at 7 Might or otherwise, because kill effects don't compare against Might.

Two caveats: if the "kill" is delivered as damage (e.g. "deal damage to a unit"), she's safe while not in combat — only a Combat Showdown with her as Attacker/Defender counts as "in combat" (FAQ 12299). And if the effect says "all units at battlefields" it never targets her, so targeting restrictions are irrelevant either way.

question: Can I use Forge of the fluft to equip blade of the ruined king without killing a unit?
answer:
Yes — Forge of the Fluft's granted ability just Attaches the Equipment; it never has you pay the Equip cost, so the "Kill a friendly unit" clause on Blade of the Ruined King is never invoked.

Forge of the Fluft gives friendly legends "[E]: Attach an Equipment you control to a unit you control." That's a bare Attach action (CR 435), not the Equip ability — no cost from the Equipment's rules text is referenced or paid. The kill requirement lives entirely inside Blade of the Ruined King's [Equip] cost (Rule 818.1.c.3), so it only matters if you activate the normal Equip ability. You still need to have played the Blade from hand normally (3 energy + 1 Order power) first; Forge just moves it, and it can even pull it off a unit it's already attached to since the granted ability lives on the battlefield rather than the now-inactive gear (Rules 718.2, 818.5.a).

question: If an opponent controls an Elder Dragon, and I control a unit which has more might than the elder: Then, I play Rampage, which deals damage to each other's units. Then does my unit die to elder because it counts as damage done by the elder, or does it survive because it doesn't count because it counts as damage done my my spell?
answer:
Your unit dies. Rampage has the two units deal damage to each other, and CR 418.6.b.3 makes the unit itself the source of that damage — so the hit your unit takes is damage marked by your opponent, i.e. "their damage," not yours. Elder Dragon's passive alters lethal damage for exactly that damage (Rule 142.4.c), so any non-zero amount is enough to kill an enemy unit regardless of Might; your unit having more Might than the Dragon is irrelevant. Counter Strike or another prevent effect would be the only thing that saves it, since prevented damage is never dealt.

Note the reverse direction still works in your favor: the damage your unit deals to Elder Dragon is your damage, so the passive doesn't protect it — if your unit's Might exceeds 10, Elder Dragon dies too (both die in the same cleanup).

question: If you activate "The List" then return it back to hand, Replay "The List" and target the same unit. Does the Minus Might Stack
answer:
Yes — the -2 [M] stacks. Each activation of The List creates its own "this turn" modifier on the unit, and nothing about The List leaving the board removes the first one.

The List's ability is [T]: Give a unit with the named tag -2 [M] this turn. Once that resolves, the -2 sits on the targeted unit for the rest of the turn regardless of what happens to The List (no "while I'm on the board" clause). Returning it to hand and replaying it makes The List a new object, but the unit is unchanged, so the new activation applies a second, separate modifier — the two are summed in the Might layer for a net -4 [M].

Two practical notes: when you replay it you re-name a tag as it's played, so just name the same tag again, and a non-unit Gear enters ready (Rule 359.2.d), so it can be exhausted for the second activation. This is also the only way to fire it twice in a turn, since the [T] cost exhausts it and gears don't ready on their own.

question: Does thwonk trigger radiant dawn twice
answer:
Yes — as long as the two stuns land on two different attacking units. Thwonk!'s Repeat lets the spell execute its effect a second time, and those executions resolve as separate, sequential game actions (game actions are never simultaneous, Rule 303.2), so Radiant Dawn's "when you stun one or more enemy units" condition is met twice, generating two buffs.

The catch is the target: a unit that's already stunned can't be stunned again, so if there's only one attacking unit, the second execution does nothing and you only get one trigger and one buff. With two (or more) attacking units you stun each on a separate execution and get two buffs. Note each buff still lands on a friendly unit of your choice, and no unit can hold more than one buff.

question: How is cauculated the Split damage from Alpha strike
answer:
Split damage from Alpha Strike is calculated at resolution, not when you play it.

At finalization you choose the friendly unit and the targets — you can pick at most as many enemy units as that unit's Might at that moment (Rule 355.14.c). When the spell actually resolves, you take the chosen unit's current Might (including any buffs granted in the meantime), then divide that total among the locked-in targets, choosing the split at that point (Rule 355.14.e). Each target must get at least 1, so if the Might dropped between finalization and resolution and there's now more targets than damage, you choose which targets cease being targets — but you can't leave fewer targets than you have damage to divide (Rule 355.14.h).

Bonus damage (e.g. from Annie, Fiery) adds to the total before you split it, not +1 per target (Rule 715.3).

question: I can react temporary sprite in beginner step playing Janna and win by hold?
answer:
Yes — as long as you control that battlefield. Janna, Savior has [Reaction], so she can be played during the Closed state created by the Sprite's Temporary trigger in your Beginning Step, and she'll be placed at that battlefield (units played at Reaction still go to your Base or a battlefield you control — Rule 813.3.a).

She resolves first off the chain, then the Temporary trigger resolves and kills the Sprite. Since Janna is still sitting there, you never lose Control, so you Hold the battlefield in the Scoring Step (CR 190.4.a, 471.2). Same interaction as reacting with a hidden Teemo (FAQ #1199).

Two notes: this must be the battlefield you control — you can't drop her onto a contested or enemy battlefield, so it won't work if the Sprite was there without you actually controlling it. And a Hold point at match point does win the game; the "score every battlefield" restriction only applies to a Final Point gained through Conquer (CR 473.1.a.1).

question: does opponent need to pay the deflect 3 twice if he targets kkayle using bellows repeat 1?
answer:
Yes — if Kayle is chosen in both executions, the deflect cost is paid twice: 3 once for the initial effect and 3 again for the repeated effect, 6 Power total (any Domain).

Each execution of Bellows Breath makes its own choices (rule 820.2.a), so the repeat execution choosing Kayle is a second "time they choose me," which is what rule 809.1.c charges for. Note the base cost is unaffected — she still takes 1 from each execution for 2 total, and the Deflect power can be any Domain.

Caveat: the deflect cost is a mandatory additional cost paid as you play the spell, so those targets and payments are locked in up front (rule 356.2.a.2). If the caster declines the Repeat cost, or repeats but chooses Kayle only in the first execution, Deflect 3 is paid just once. (One older FAQ entry claims Deflect is once-per-spell; the current Core Rules wording and the bulk of FAQ rulings go per choosing.)

question: if playing darius legend. and you have 1 energy. you have a hidden kennen keeper of balance at a battlefield. you flip it, tap legend. then use that to pay the 2 to stun. is this allowed? does this order work? can you use kennen to trigger legion on legend to then pay for that same kennen?

Legion on Hand of Noxus checks whether a card other than the one with the Legion ability has been finalized this turn (Rule 812.1.c), and Darius is a Legend that's never played, so Kennen being finalized satisfies it. Kennen's "When you play me" trigger uses the resolve meaning of play, so by the time it asks for the [2], Kennen has already been finalized and Legion is active.

You can then exhaust Darius mid-resolution: activated abilities that Add resources and have Reaction may be activated any time a spell or ability requires resources be paid, and they finalize and resolve immediately, even during another effect's resolution (CR 430.3, 445.2.c). So your 1 floating energy + Darius's 1 = the [2], and the stun happens (same pattern as paying Hard Bargain's [2] with Darius).

Two caveats: tapping Darius before playing Kennen does nothing — with no card played that turn, Legion isn't met and no energy is added. And since Kennen was played from Hidden, the "when you play me" stun must target a unit at the battlefield where he was hidden.

So there's no window where the trigger sits on the chain unpaid while you wait for an opponent's reaction. The good news is you don't need one: Darius's legend ability adds resources with Reaction, and resource-adding abilities finalize and resolve immediately any time a cost must be paid (CR 430.3, 445.2.c). Two things to confirm: Darius's Legion condition is met because Kennen himself was played this turn (Legion checks Finalized cards, CR 420.4.b), and if you decline to pay, the trigger is removed from the chain as if it never happened (Rule 383.3.a.2). question: My opponents acitvates baited hook- in response i play a thrill of the hunt on my brynhir- is my enemy allowed to play the card from hook ?
answer:
No — if Thrill of the Hunt resolves, the Baited Hook player gets nothing off the hook.

Sequence: Thrill of the Hunt is on the chain above Baited Hook, so it resolves first, banishing and replaying Brynhir. Brynhir finalizes, its "when you play me" trigger goes on the chain above the still-unresolved Baited Hook ability and resolves first, locking opponents out of playing cards for the rest of the turn. Baited Hook then resolves with the lock already in place: the kill still happens and they still look at the top 5, but the "play it" instruction is skipped as impossible (Rule 358.3.a — a "can't" effect beats the permission), so the 5 cards are recycled.

The one window they have is before Thrill of the Hunt resolves: if they respond by killing/removing Brynhir, Thrill of the Hunt mistargets, Brynhir never re-enters, and Baited Hook works normally. Removing Brynhir after the trigger is on the chain doesn't help them — the trigger is independent (FAQ #2283); they'd have to counter the trigger itself.

One requirement: Zhonya's must already be face-up when the damage happens, since it's a replacement effect and not a trigger. question: does reacting with tactical retreat prevent cull the weak ?
answer:
Yes — Tactical Retreat saves the unit. It's a replacement effect ("the next time it would die this turn, heal it, exhaust it, and recall it instead"), so it intercedes when Cull's kill happens and the unit is recalled to base instead of dying (Rules 369–370).

question: If I attack into a battlefield with Kennen - Keeper of Balance and a Vi - Peacekeeper, stunning my opponent's Astral Heron with the Vi but they also have a Tornado Warrior at the battlefield, will my Kennen die after the combat if they assign the 3 damage to my Kennen since the stunned unit will die during combat damage step and thus lose his +2 might?
answer:
No — Kennen survives. Astral Heron dying doesn't retroactively make the 3 damage lethal on Kennen.

Here's why: Kennen's +2 is a static ability, and the stunned Astral Heron is still sitting at that battlefield for the entire combat (stun only clears in the end-of-turn cleanup, 423.1.a.2). So all combat math is done with Kennen at 4 [M], and the defending player's 3 damage is simply not lethal on a 4-Might unit.

The kill from combat damage happens in the Combat Cleanup, and that check is a single simultaneous batch — "all units with lethal damage marked are killed" (CR 323.4). Astral Heron is still on the board at the moment that check is made, so Kennen is still 4 [M] and isn't in the batch. Then the same cleanup heals every unit in play (466.1.a.1), wiping the 3 damage off Kennen before anything else can check it.

One note: to actually kill Kennen in this combat they'd have to assign 4 damage, not 3 — and the defending player only has 3 damage to work with here since the stunned Heron contributes nothing (423.1.b).
